query.original_query: subliminal learning hidden trait transmission channel capacity data-free distillation

sub_queries.semantic_query: knowledge distillation without data, hidden representation transmission, channel capacity of internal features, subliminal learning in neural networks, information bottleneck and feature leakage
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the phenomenon of knowledge transfer between neural networks through the analysis of hidden representation transmission in the absence of original training data. Using a causal mediation framework, we examine how internal feature channels in a teacher model encode task-relevant information and the extent to which this information can be decoded by a student model from compressed representations. Our analysis reveals that feature leakage through the information bottleneck is not uniform across layers; deeper representations exhibit higher channel capacity but also greater redundancy, limiting the fidelity of reconstruction. We find that student models trained solely on transmitted hidden states can recover substantial task performance, suggesting that subliminal learning occurs via the preservation of sparse, monosemantic features within the residual stream. Results show that the efficacy of this distillation depends critically on the alignment between the teacher’s feature activation patterns and the student’s architectural capacity, with attention heads and MLP layers contributing differentially to the transmitted signal. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the feasibility of data-free knowledge distillation and the role of internal representation structure in cross-model information transfer.

sub_queries.semantic_query: subliminal learning implicit memory acquisition, hidden trait transmission, channel capacity of unconscious information processing, perceptual learning without awareness, feature extraction under limited attention
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether subliminally presented statistical regularities can be acquired without awareness and subsequently influence explicit task performance. Participants completed a modified serial reaction time task in which a hidden sequence of target locations was embedded within a stream of masked, briefly presented stimuli. Awareness was assessed through both subjective confidence ratings and objective forced-choice recognition tests. We measured response time facilitation and error rates as indices of implicit learning, and employed multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) on EEG data to track neural representations of the hidden sequence. Results indicate that participants showed significant response time savings for the embedded sequence despite chance-level recognition performance, consistent with implicit memory acquisition. Furthermore, MVPA revealed distinct neural signatures in occipital and parietal electrodes during subliminal sequence presentation, suggesting that feature extraction occurred without attentional engagement. Findings support the hypothesis that the unconscious processing system has a measurable channel capacity for extracting and retaining structural information, and that such learning can occur independently of explicit awareness.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Knowledge Transfer via Distillation of Activation Boundaries Formed by Hidden Neurons
papers.research_question: Can transferring activation boundaries (whether neurons are activated or not), rather than the magnitude of neuron responses, improve knowledge transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a knowledge transfer method that distills activation boundaries (neuron on/off states) from teacher to student networks, outperforming existing methods by focusing on boundary information rather than response magnitudes.
papers.conclusion: Activation boundaries are important for knowledge transfer, and the proposed method of transferring these boundaries significantly improves performance over state-of-the-art methods, potentially changing neural network training practices.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method accelerates learning and improves generalization, especially with limited training data.
It outperforms existing knowledge transfer methods (FITNET, FSP, AT, Jacobian) in various settings including learning speed, small data, and network compression.
In transfer learning, the proposed method sometimes outperforms ImageNet pre-training.
The method is effective across different network layers (low, mid, high).
The proposed alternative loss effectively approximates the ideal activation transfer loss, leading to high similarity in neuron activations between teacher and student.
future_direction: Applying the method to various tasks that originally relied on pre-training for better performance and learning speed.
papers.abstract: An activation boundary for a neuron refers to a separating hyperplane that determines whether the neuron is activated or deactivated. It has been long considered in neural networks that the activations of neurons, rather than their exact output values, play the most important role in forming classificationfriendly partitions of the hidden feature space. However, as far as we know, this aspect of neural networks has not been considered in the literature of knowledge transfer. In this paper, we propose a knowledge transfer method via distillation of activation boundaries formed by hidden neurons. For the distillation, we propose an activation transfer loss that has the minimum value when the boundaries generated by the student coincide with those by the teacher. Since the activation transfer loss is not differentiable, we design a piecewise differentiable loss approximating the activation transfer loss. By the proposed method, the student learns a separating boundary between activation region and deactivation region formed by each neuron in the teacher. Through the experiments in various aspects of knowledge transfer, it is verified that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: Information Flow in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can information theory and the Information Bottleneck framework be used to understand and improve deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis introduces the dual Information Bottleneck (dualIB) framework and provides an information-theoretic analysis of deep neural networks, showing they optimize the Information Bottleneck trade-off and that the dualIB improves prediction for finite data.
papers.conclusion: The thesis proposes a new information-theoretic perspective for studying deep neural networks, which can lead to a deeper understanding, explain their behavior, and improve their performance, while opening new theoretical and practical research questions.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks optimize each layer's mutual information on input and output, resulting in a trade-off between compression and prediction.
Stochastic gradient descent follows the Information Bottleneck trade-off in two phases: a fast empirical error minimization phase followed by a slow representation compression phase.
For infinite ensembles of infinitely-wide neural networks, information-theoretic quantities can be computed in closed form via the network's kernels.
The dual Information Bottleneck framework resolves some drawbacks of the original IB and optimizes the mean prediction error exponent.
A variational dualIB framework enables practical application to real-world datasets using deep neural networks.
papers.limitation:
Estimating mutual information in high-dimensional spaces is computationally challenging.
The Information Bottleneck framework is non-parametric and assumes full access to the joint probability distribution, which is often not available.
future_direction: Further investigation of the connection between compression and generalization in deep neural networks.
Exploration of multi-domain, semi-supervised representation learning using information-theoretic principles.
Study of the computational benefits of hidden layers in deep networks and the trade-off with finite-sample learning.
Analysis of the finite-sample information plane and its relationship to optimization dynamics.
Further development and evaluation of the variational dualIB framework on larger datasets and different architectures.
Adaptation of information-theoretic learning principles to biologically plausible deep learning models.
papers.abstract: Although deep neural networks have been immensely successful, there is no comprehensive theoretical understanding of how they work or are structured. As a result, deep networks are often seen as black boxes with unclear interpretations and reliability. Understanding the performance of deep neural networks is one of the greatest scientific challenges. This work aims to apply principles and techniques from information theory to deep learning models to increase our theoretical understanding and design better algorithms. We first describe our information-theoretic approach to deep learning. Then, we propose using the Information Bottleneck (IB) theory to explain deep learning systems. The novel paradigm for analyzing networks sheds light on their layered structure, generalization abilities, and learning dynamics. We later discuss one of the most challenging problems of applying the IB to deep neural networks - estimating mutual information. Recent theoretical developments, such as the neural tangent kernel (NTK) framework, are used to investigate generalization signals. In our study, we obtained tractable computations of many information-theoretic quantities and their bounds for infinite ensembles of infinitely wide neural networks. With these derivations, we can determine how compression, generalization, and sample size pertain to the network and how they are related. At the end, we present the dual Information Bottleneck (dualIB). This new information-theoretic framework resolves some of the IB's shortcomings by merely switching terms in the distortion function. The dualIB can account for known data features and use them to make better predictions over unseen examples. An analytical framework reveals the underlying structure and optimal representations, and a variational framework using deep neural network optimization validates the results.

papers.title: Deep learning and the information bottleneck principle
papers.research_question: How can deep neural networks be analyzed using the information bottleneck principle to understand their architecture, generalization, and optimality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an information theoretic analysis of deep neural networks using the information bottleneck principle, providing theoretical limits on efficiency, generalization bounds, and insights into layered architecture.
papers.conclusion: The information bottleneck principle provides a framework for analyzing deep neural networks, offering advantages in evaluating layers, deriving optimization criteria, generalization bounds, and linking architecture to information theoretic phase transitions.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs can be quantified by the mutual information between layers and the input/output variables, allowing comparison to optimal information bottleneck limits.
The information bottleneck principle offers new optimization criteria for DNN representations based on compression and prediction trade-offs.
Finite sample generalization bounds can be derived from the information bottleneck, indicating the need for compression for better generalization.
There is a conjectured connection between information bottleneck phase transitions and the breakdown of linear separability, relating to DNN layer structure.
Stochastic DNN architectures may achieve closer proximity to the optimal information bottleneck limit compared to deterministic ones.
future_direction: Further exploration of the connection between network architecture and structural phase transitions in the information bottleneck problem.
Development of new training algorithms based on information bottleneck optimality conditions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are analyzed via the theoretical framework of the information bottleneck (IB) principle. We first show that any DNN can be quantified by the mutual information between the layers and the input and output variables. Using this representation we can calculate the optimal information theoretic limits of the DNN and obtain finite sample generalization bounds. The advantage of getting closer to the theoretical limit is quantifiable both by the generalization bound and by the network's simplicity. We argue that both the optimal architecture, number of layers and features/connections at each layer, are related to the bifurcation points of the information bottleneck tradeoff, namely, relevant compression of the input layer with respect to the output layer. The hierarchical representations at the layered network naturally correspond to the structural phase transitions along the information curve. We believe that this new insight can lead to new optimality bounds and deep learning algorithms.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Flow of Information in Feed-Forward Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does the entropy of information change between consecutive layers in a feed-forward deep neural network, and how can the training process be formulated as an optimization problem based on the Information Bottleneck principle?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops an information-theoretic framework to analyze the flow of information in feed-forward deep neural networks, formulates the training process as a constrained optimization problem based on the Information Bottleneck principle, and proves an upper bound on the total compression achievable with an acceptable level of distortion.
papers.conclusion: The paper uses information theory to study information flow in DNNs, models the learning process as an optimization problem, and proves an upper bound on compression. Future work aims to extend the analysis to broader learning problems and continuous input/output spaces.
papers.key_findings:
The entropy of information decreases between consecutive layers by the expected entropy of the partitions on the layer's input space (Lemma 1).
The conditional entropy of each layer, conditioned on the desired output, is also a non-increasing function across layers (Lemma 2).
The maximum possible entropy reduction (total compression) in a DNN is bounded by H(X|Y) - H(Xν|Y), and in the limit of zero distortion, cannot exceed H(X|Y) (Lemma 3).
The learning process of a feed-forward DNN can be modeled as a convex optimization problem that maximizes a weighted sum of entropy reductions subject to a distortion constraint.
A modified optimization problem is proposed to exclude mappings that are unfeasible due to the structural limitations of individual neurons (e.g., the XOR function).
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes the neural network is used for supervised learning tasks and the input/output spaces are based on discrete alphabets.
Due to the structural limitations of an artificial neuron (e.g., implementing only linearly separable functions), not all mappings determined by the initial optimization problem are feasible for implementation with a single layer.
future_direction: Extend the work to a broader range of learning problems and include continuous input/output spaces in the model.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward deep neural networks have been used extensively in various machine learning applications. Developing a precise understanding of the underling behavior of neural networks is crucial for their efficient deployment. In this paper, we use an information theoretic approach to study the flow of information in a neural network and to determine how entropy of information changes between consecutive layers. Moreover, using the Information Bottleneck principle, we develop a constrained optimization problem that can be used in the training process of a deep neural network. Furthermore, we determine a lower bound for the level of data representation that can be achieved in a deep neural network with an acceptable level of distortion.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information
papers.research_question: How do deep neural networks organize information during training, and do they optimize the Information Bottleneck tradeoff between compression and prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that DNN training has two distinct phases: empirical error minimization and representation compression, and that the converged layers lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck theoretical bound.
papers.conclusion: Deep Learning with DNNs are in essence learning algorithms that effectively find efficient representations that are approximate minimal sufficient statistics in the Information Bottleneck sense.
papers.key_findings:
Stochastic Gradient Descent optimization has two phases: a drift phase (empirical error minimization) and a diffusion phase (representation compression).
The converged layers of DNNs lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck bound, satisfying the self-consistent equations.
Adding hidden layers dramatically reduces the number of training epochs required for good generalization, indicating a computational benefit.
The compression phase is responsible for the absence of overfitting in deep learning.
The hidden layers appear to converge to critical points on the Information Bottleneck curve.
papers.limitation: The findings need to be verified on larger networks, other architectures, and real-world problems.
future_direction: Developing new learning algorithms that utilize the claimed IB optimality of the layers.
Combining IB iterations with stochastic relaxation methods to boost DNN training.
papers.abstract: Despite their great success, there is still no comprehensive theoretical understanding of learning with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) or their inner organization. Previous work proposed to analyze DNNs in the \textit{Information Plane}; i.e., the plane of the Mutual Information values that each layer preserves on the input and output variables. They suggested that the goal of the network is to optimize the Information Bottleneck (IB) tradeoff between compression and prediction, successively, for each layer. In this work we follow up on this idea and demonstrate the effectiveness of the Information-Plane visualization of DNNs. Our main results are: (i) most of the training epochs in standard DL are spent on {\emph compression} of the input to efficient representation and not on fitting the training labels. (ii) The representation compression phase begins when the training errors becomes small and the Stochastic Gradient Decent (SGD) epochs change from a fast drift to smaller training error into a stochastic relaxation, or random diffusion, constrained by the training error value. (iii) The converged layers lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck (IB) theoretical bound, and the maps from the input to any hidden layer and from this hidden layer to the output satisfy the IB self-consistent equations. This generalization through noise mechanism is unique to Deep Neural Networks and absent in one layer networks. (iv) The training time is dramatically reduced when adding more hidden layers. Thus the main advantage of the hidden layers is computational. This can be explained by the reduced relaxation time, as this it scales super-linearly (exponentially for simple diffusion) with the information compression from the previous layer.

papers.title: Entropy and mutual information in models of deep neural networks*
papers.research_question: How can we compute entropies and mutual information in deep neural networks, and what do these quantities reveal about the relationship between compression and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a replica formula to compute entropies and mutual information in stochastic deep neural networks with orthogonally-invariant weights, provides a rigorous proof for two-layer Gaussian networks, and proposes an experimental framework with USV-layers to study compression and generalization.
papers.conclusion: In the proposed setting, the relationship between compression (as measured by mutual information) and generalization remains elusive.
papers.key_findings:
The replica formula provides accurate estimates of entropies and mutual information for large networks, outperforming non-parametric estimators.
For bounded activation functions (e.g., hardtanh), entropies decrease after a certain weight scale, while for unbounded ones (e.g., ReLU) they monotonically increase.
In linear networks trained with USV-layers, mutual information between input and hidden layers increases throughout learning without harming generalization.
In non-linear networks on correlated data, the expected compression-generalization relationship (information bottleneck) is not clearly observed.
The proposed USV-layers allow the replica formula to remain valid during learning, enabling the study of information-theoretic quantities.
papers.limitation:
The assumption of orthogonally-invariant weight matrices is restrictive and may not hold in general.
The addition of small Gaussian noise to compute mutual information is arbitrary and may affect the results.
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine a class of stochastic deep learning models with a tractable method to compute information-theoretic quantities. Our contributions are three-fold: (i) we show how entropies and mutual informations can be derived from heuristic statistical physics methods, under the assumption that weight matrices are independent and orthogonally-invariant. (ii) We extend particular cases in which this result is known to be rigorously exact by providing a proof for two-layers networks with Gaussian random weights, using the recently introduced adaptive interpolation method. (iii) We propose an experiment framework with generative models of synthetic datasets, on which we train deep neural networks with a weight constraint designed so that the assumption in (i) is verified during learning. We study the behavior of entropies and mutual informations throughout learning and conclude that, in the proposed setting, the relationship between compression and generalization remains elusive.

papers.title: Measuring Information Transfer in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How to measure the generalizable information in a neural network model? The paper proposes a measure called Information Transfer (LIT) based on prequential coding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Information Transfer (LIT), a measure based on prequential coding, to estimate the generalizable information in a neural network model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Information Transfer (LIT) is a practical measure of generalizable information in neural networks and can serve as a useful tool for analyzing deep learning problems from an information perspective.
papers.key_findings:
LIT is consistently correlated with generalizable information and can be used as a measure of patterns or knowledge in a model or dataset.
LIT can dissect the information content of a dataset, as shown in the CIFAR-10 subtasks analysis.
In transfer learning, the Information Advantage (LIA) derived from LIT measures the quality of pre-trained representation models.
In continual learning, LIT measures the information preserved about past tasks, revealing that catastrophic forgetting is less severe in terms of information loss than performance metrics suggest.
LIT provides an information perspective that helps discover new insights into neural network learning, such as the dynamics of information transfer and forgetting.
papers.limitation: The quality of the approximation is hard to guarantee theoretically due to lack of analysis on convergence properties of prequential coding.
future_direction: Develop learning algorithms to maximize generalizable model knowledge.
papers.abstract: Quantifying the information content in a neural network model is essentially estimating the model's Kolmogorov complexity. Recent success of prequential coding on neural networks points to a promising path of deriving an efficient description length of a model. We propose a practical measure of the generalizable information in a neural network model based on prequential coding, which we term Information Transfer ($L_{IT}$). Theoretically, $L_{IT}$ is an estimation of the generalizable part of a model's information content. In experiments, we show that $L_{IT}$ is consistently correlated with generalizable information and can be used as a measure of patterns or "knowledge" in a model or a dataset. Consequently, $L_{IT}$ can serve as a useful analysis tool in deep learning. In this paper, we apply $L_{IT}$ to compare and dissect information in datasets, evaluate representation models in transfer learning, and analyze catastrophic forgetting and continual learning algorithms. $L_{IT}$ provides an information perspective which helps us discover new insights into neural network learning.

papers.title: Estimating Information Flow in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we accurately estimate the mutual information between the input and internal representations of a deep neural network, and what geometric phenomenon (clustering) underlies the observed compression of mutual information during training?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a rigorous framework for accurate estimation of mutual information in noisy DNNs and identifies geometric clustering of internal representations as the driver of compression, clarifying that binning-based measures in prior work track clustering rather than mutual information.
papers.conclusion: Clustering of internal representations is the fundamental geometric phenomenon of interest, which occurs in both deterministic and noisy networks; mutual information is only meaningful in the presence of noise and tracks the same clustering effect, while binning-based measures are simple proxies for clustering.
papers.key_findings:
In deterministic DNNs, mutual information I(X; Tℓ) is vacuous (infinite or constant), so the compression observed via binning in prior works actually measures clustering of representations.
In noisy DNNs, compression of I(X; Tℓ) during training is driven by progressive geometric clustering of representations from the same class.
Clustering of internal representations occurs in both deterministic and noisy DNNs, and can be measured by the discrete entropy H(Bin(Tℓ)).
The relationship between compression (or clustering) and generalization performance is not straightforward and may not be causal.
The proposed Sample Propagation estimator provides a theoretically grounded method for estimating mutual information in noisy DNNs.
papers.limitation:
Mutual information estimation is statistically difficult and requires a number of samples that can be exponential in the dimension of the hidden layer.
The binning-based measure H(Bin(Tℓ)) is not an accurate estimator of mutual information and its interpretation depends on the bin size.
future_direction: Develop efficient methods to track clustering in high-dimensional spaces.
Investigate the connection between clustering and generalization theoretically and experimentally.
Develop a new regularization procedure for DNN training that encourages intermediate layers to increase a clustering-based analog of I(Y; Tℓ).
papers.abstract: We study the flow of information and the evolution of internal representations during deep neural network (DNN) training, aiming to demystify the compression aspect of the information bottleneck theory. The theory suggests that DNN training comprises a rapid fitting phase followed by a slower compression phase, in which the mutual information $I(X;T)$ between the input $X$ and internal representations $T$ decreases. Several papers observe compression of estimated mutual information on different DNN models, but the true $I(X;T)$ over these networks is provably either constant (discrete $X$) or infinite (continuous $X$). This work explains the discrepancy between theory and experiments, and clarifies what was actually measured by these past works. To this end, we introduce an auxiliary (noisy) DNN framework for which $I(X;T)$ is a meaningful quantity that depends on the network's parameters. This noisy framework is shown to be a good proxy for the original (deterministic) DNN both in terms of performance and the learned representations. We then develop a rigorous estimator for $I(X;T)$ in noisy DNNs and observe compression in various models. By relating $I(X;T)$ in the noisy DNN to an information-theoretic communication problem, we show that compression is driven by the progressive clustering of hidden representations of inputs from the same class. Several methods to directly monitor clustering of hidden representations, both in noisy and deterministic DNNs, are used to show that meaningful clusters form in the $T$ space. Finally, we return to the estimator of $I(X;T)$ employed in past works, and demonstrate that while it fails to capture the true (vacuous) mutual information, it does serve as a measure for clustering. This clarifies the past observations of compression and isolates the geometric clustering of hidden representations as the true phenomenon of interest.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers.research_question: Can distilling internal representations (attention probabilities and hidden states) in addition to soft labels improve knowledge distillation, especially for compressing large teacher models into smaller students?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes distilling internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) of a large teacher model into a smaller student, which consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation and better preserves the teacher's internal behavior.
papers.conclusion: Internal knowledge distillation effectively compresses a large model into a smaller one while preserving similar performance and the internal behavior of the teacher, outperforming standard distillation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge distillation (using attention and hidden state losses) consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation across GLUE datasets.
The method achieves significant parameter reduction (e.g., 50% for BERT6) while maintaining performance close to the teacher.
Internal distillation is more resilient than standard distillation when training data size is reduced.
The student can learn internal representations effectively even before training the classification layer, as shown in progressive distillation experiments.
The student's internal attention behavior becomes more similar to the teacher's, whereas standard distillation leads to different internal representations.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Distillation Dynamics: Towards Understanding Feature-Based Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-based knowledge distillation, which works well for CNNs, fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), and what is the root cause of negative transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern (compression followed by expansion) and identifies a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models as the root cause of negative transfer in feature-based distillation, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViT compression strategies.
papers.conclusion: Successful knowledge transfer in Vision Transformers requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect the fundamental representational constraints and the U-shaped information processing dynamics of these architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT models exhibit a learned U-shaped pattern in information entropy and activation magnitude across layers, indicating an initial compression phase followed by a task-specific expansion phase.
The failure of feature-based distillation in ViTs stems from a representational mismatch: teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity.
Late-layer feature alignment actively harms student performance (negative transfer) because it forces the student to adopt a representational paradigm incompatible with its capacity, disrupting its natural learning progression.
Frequency spectrum analysis shows teacher ViTs transition from low-pass to uniform, high-energy spectra in late layers, while CNNs maintain low-pass spectra, explaining why feature mimicry works for CNNs but fails for ViTs.
The U-shaped information processing signature is a consistent learned behavior across different ViT architectures (e.g., CaiT, standard ViT) and training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised like MAE).
papers.abstract: While feature-based knowledge distillation has proven highly effective for compressing CNNs, these techniques unexpectedly fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), often performing worse than simple logit-based distillation. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of this phenomenon through a novel analytical framework termed as "distillation dynamics", combining frequency spectrum analysis, information entropy metrics, and activation magnitude tracking. Our investigation reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern: initial compression followed by expansion. We identify the root cause of negative transfer in feature distillation: a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models. Through frequency-domain analysis, we show that teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding strategies in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity. This mismatch causes late-layer feature alignment to actively harm student performance. Our findings reveal that successful knowledge transfer in ViTs requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect these fundamental representational constraints, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViTs compression strategies. All source code and experimental logs are provided at https://github.com/thy960112/Distillation-Dynamics.

papers.title: Understanding Autoencoders with Information Theoretic Concepts
papers.research_question: How can information theory be used to understand the dynamics of learning and the design of autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an information-theoretic methodology to understand autoencoders, including three fundamental properties about layer-wise information flow and intrinsic dimensionality, validated experimentally.
papers.conclusion: Information theory provides a powerful framework for understanding autoencoders, with implications for optimal design, training methods, and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The first type of Data Processing Inequality (DPI) holds for encoder and decoder layers: I(X; T1) ≥ I(X; T2) ≥ ... and I(X'; T1') ≥ I(X'; T2') ≥ ...
The second type of DPI holds for mutual information between corresponding layers: I(X; X') ≥ I(T1; T1') ≥ ... ≥ H(Z).
There exists a bifurcation point in the information plane when the bottleneck layer size equals the intrinsic dimensionality of the data.
The matrix-based Renyi's entropy functional is an effective estimator for mutual information in high dimensions.
The information flow in autoencoders reveals two phases of learning: fitting the data manifold and fine-tuning representations.
papers.limitation:
The estimator requires careful selection of the kernel size parameter.
The intrinsic dimensionality is an effective measure without rigorous physical meaning.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to other DNN architectures like CNNs.
Investigate the physical meaning of intrinsic dimensionality.
papers.abstract: Despite their great success in practical applications, there is still a lack of theoretical and systematic methods to analyze deep neural networks. In this paper, we illustrate an advanced information theoretic methodology to understand the dynamics of learning and the design of autoencoders, a special type of deep learning architectures that resembles a communication channel. By generalizing the information plane to any cost function, and inspecting the roles and dynamics of different layers using layer-wise information quantities, we emphasize the role that mutual information plays in quantifying learning from data. We further suggest and also experimentally validate, for mean square error training, three fundamental properties regarding the layer-wise flow of information and intrinsic dimensionality of the bottleneck layer, using respectively the data processing inequality and the identification of a bifurcation point in the information plane that is controlled by the given data. Our observations have a direct impact on the optimal design of autoencoders, the design of alternative feedforward training methods, and even in the problem of generalization.

papers.title: Information Bottleneck: Exact Analysis of (Quantized) Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Are the fitting and compression phases in information bottleneck analysis of neural networks real or artifacts of binning when estimating mutual information?
papers.core_contribution: By using quantized neural networks, mutual information can be computed exactly, showing that fitting and compression phases in IB analysis are not artifacts of binning but depend on network architecture and activation functions.
papers.conclusion: The exact IB analysis confirms that compression phase depends on network architecture, and the proposed framework allows for accurate future studies of IB phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Both fitting and compression phases occur in the output SOFTMAX layer for both TANH and RELU networks.
For hidden layers, fitting occurs for both TANH and RELU, but compression is only observed in the last hidden layer for TANH and not for RELU.
More complex networks with many neurons do not exhibit compression because they are too expressive.
Exact MI computation eliminates measurement artifacts, allowing future research to focus on the utility of IB.
papers.limitation:
The study could not resolve the controversy about the compression phase because it depends on the network architecture.
Studying continuous systems would lead to trivial results, so quantization is used but is not a conceptual limitation.
future_direction: Focus on utility of IB principle for understanding learning dynamics
Accurate future studies of IB phenomena using the proposed framework
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck (IB) principle has been suggested as a way to analyze deep neural networks. The learning dynamics are studied by inspecting the mutual information (MI) between the hidden layers and the input and output. Notably, separate fitting and compression phases during training have been reported. This led to some controversy including claims that the observations are not reproducible and strongly dependent on the type of activation function used as well as on the way the MI is estimated. Our study confirms that different ways of binning when computing the MI lead to qualitatively different results, either supporting or refusing IB conjectures. To resolve the controversy, we study the IB principle in settings where MI is non-trivial and can be computed exactly. We monitor the dynamics of quantized neural networks, that is, we discretize the whole deep learning system so that no approximation is required when computing the MI. This allows us to quantify the information flow without measurement errors. In this setting, we observed a fitting phase for all layers and a compression phase for the output layer in all experiments; the compression in the hidden layers was dependent on the type of activation function. Our study shows that the initial IB results were not artifacts of binning when computing the MI. However, the critical claim that the compression phase may not be observed for some networks also holds true.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How discriminative are individual CNN features for characterizing classes across different datasets, and how can they be used for knowledge representation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both their presence and absence, and that convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: CNN features, especially from convolutional layers, are highly discriminative and can be used for knowledge representation by both presence and absence, with context being key in the feature extraction process.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their presence or their absence, providing two modalities of information.
Convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously considered, opening their use for knowledge representation and unsupervised learning.
Low and middle level features behave similarly across datasets, indicating they can be used for knowledge representation on a wide variety of datasets without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly tied to the similarity between the source and target tasks; for dissimilar tasks, they behave similarly to convolutional features.
A thresholding method based on statistical distance can be applied to remove noisy features, with the threshold correlated to the number of images per class.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: A Measure of the Complexity of Neural Representations based on Partial Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How is task-relevant information distributed among neurons in a neural network, and how can we quantify the difficulty of accessing information spread across multiple neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces representational complexity, a measure of information sparsity in neural representations derived from partial information decomposition, and shows that it decreases over training and through successive layers in quantized neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Representational complexity is a principled and interpretable summary statistic for analyzing the structure and evolution of neural representations in complex systems.
papers.key_findings:
Representational complexity decreases through successive hidden layers.
Representational complexity decreases over training.
Representational complexity is higher on the test dataset than on the train dataset in later stages of training.
In the case of overfitting (shuffled labels), the gap between train and test representational complexity is wide.
Representational complexity provides a target-oriented measure compared to intrinsic dimensionality.
papers.limitation:
Scaling the approach to larger networks remains a challenge; subsampling suffers from conceptual flaws and coarse-graining bounds become impractically loose for large networks.
The analysis methods are currently limited to quantized networks.
future_direction: Studying overfitting using representational complexity.
Extending the approach to larger networks by computing representational complexity without computing all PID atoms.
papers.abstract: In neural networks, task-relevant information is represented jointly by groups of neurons. However, the specific way in which this mutual information about the classification label is distributed among the individual neurons is not well understood: While parts of it may only be obtainable from specific single neurons, other parts are carried redundantly or synergistically by multiple neurons. We show how Partial Information Decomposition (PID), a recent extension of information theory, can disentangle these different contributions. From this, we introduce the measure of "Representational Complexity", which quantifies the difficulty of accessing information spread across multiple neurons. We show how this complexity is directly computable for smaller layers. For larger layers, we propose subsampling and coarse-graining procedures and prove corresponding bounds on the latter. Empirically, for quantized deep neural networks solving the MNIST and CIFAR10 tasks, we observe that representational complexity decreases both through successive hidden layers and over training, and compare the results to related measures. Overall, we propose representational complexity as a principled and interpretable summary statistic for analyzing the structure and evolution of neural representations and complex systems in general.

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: Theory of the superposition principle for randomized connectionist representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: What is the retrieval accuracy and information capacity of superposition operations in neural networks, and how can networks with recency effects be designed to avoid catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a theory for superposition operations in neural networks, mapping VSA models to RNNs and deriving retrieval accuracy and channel capacity. Proposes new models with recency effects to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: With the theory presented, neural networks based on VSAs can be appropriately scaled and optimized to handle communication or memory demands.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval accuracy of superposition can be analyzed by a single equation, and the theory matches simulations.
Networks representing information in superposition can achieve a channel capacity of about half a bit per neuron.
Existing VSA models (HDC, HRR, FHRR) exhibit the same retrieval accuracy and channel capacity.
A trained RNN does not exceed the performance of existing VSA models.
Networks with recency effects (via contracting weights or non-linearities) can form a memory buffer for infinite sequences and can be optimized for information content.
papers.abstract: To understand cognitive reasoning in the brain, it has been proposed that symbols and compositions of symbols are represented by activity patterns (vectors) in a large population of neurons. Formal models implementing this idea [Plate 2003], [Kanerva 2009], [Gayler 2003], [Eliasmith 2012] include a reversible superposition operation for representing with a single vector an entire set of symbols or an ordered sequence of symbols. If the representation space is high-dimensional, large sets of symbols can be superposed and individually retrieved. However, crosstalk noise limits the accuracy of retrieval and information capacity. To understand information processing in the brain and to design artificial neural systems for cognitive reasoning, a theory of this superposition operation is essential. Here, such a theory is presented. The superposition operations in different existing models are mapped to linear neural networks with unitary recurrent matrices, in which retrieval accuracy can be analyzed by a single equation. We show that networks representing information in superposition can achieve a channel capacity of about half a bit per neuron, a significant fraction of the total available entropy. Going beyond existing models, superposition operations with recency effects are proposed that avoid catastrophic forgetting when representing the history of infinite data streams. These novel models correspond to recurrent networks with non-unitary matrices or with nonlinear neurons, and can be analyzed and optimized with an extension of our theory.

papers.title: On information captured by neural networks: connections with memorization and generalization
papers.research_question: How does the information captured by neural networks during training relate to memorization and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation develops an information-theoretic framework to understand memorization and generalization in neural networks, introducing methods to control label noise information, measure sample informativeness, and derive nonvacuous generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization by analyzing the information captured during training.
papers.key_findings:
Limiting label noise information in neural network weights reduces memorization of noisy labels and improves generalization.
The proposed functional sample information (F-SI) measure identifies atypical, ambiguous, or underrepresented examples that are more informative for training.
The f-CMI generalization bounds, based on information in predictions, are nonvacuous and closely track the generalization gap in practical deep learning scenarios.
Knowledge distillation benefits from reducing supervision complexity, which is controlled by teacher accuracy, margin, and the compatibility of teacher and student neural tangent kernels.
Sample-wise information-theoretic generalization bounds have formal limitations, revealing a difference between information-theoretic and PAC-Bayesian perspectives.
papers.limitation: The linearized network approximation used to compute sample information may not be accurate for highly nonlinear networks or when the network is far from its initialization.
future_direction: Extending the sample information measure to other learning settings beyond classification.
Improving the f-CMI-based generalization bounds to be tighter in cases where they currently overestimate the gap.
Further exploration of online knowledge distillation and its theoretical properties.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularity and success of deep learning, there is limited understanding of when, how, and why neural networks generalize to unseen examples. Since learning can be seen as extracting information from data, we formally study information captured by neural networks during training. Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: Information Plane Analysis Visualization in Deep Learning via Transfer Entropy
papers.research_question: Does Transfer Entropy provide a better measure for Information Plane analysis to understand the link between compression and generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using Transfer Entropy (TE) instead of Mutual Information for Information Plane analysis to quantify information transfer between neural layers and investigate the link between compression and generalization.
papers.conclusion: Transfer Entropy provides a useful measure for Information Plane analysis, showing a strong connection between TE evolution and accuracy/loss, and can be used to visualize compression and fitting phases in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Entropy (TE) can be used to quantify information transfer between neural layers and perform Information Plane analysis, providing an alternative to Mutual Information.
TE values decrease during training, indicating compression of irrelevant information, and are sensitive to network architecture efficiency.
There is a strong connection between accuracy/loss and TE evolution, with TE inversely related to accuracy and closely following loss during training.
The last layers of the network show higher TE values and variance, suggesting they contain generic features and receive most variations during training.
The fitting and compression phases described in Information Bottleneck theory can be observed via TE dynamics.
future_direction: Explore the use of a TE-based loss function to enhance training of deep neural networks.
papers.abstract: In a feedforward network, Transfer Entropy (TE) can be used to measure the influence that one layer has on another by quantifying the information transfer between them during training. According to the Information Bottleneck principle, a neural model's internal representation should compress the input data as much as possible while still retaining sufficient information about the output. Information Plane analysis is a visualization technique used to understand the trade-off between compression and information preservation in the context of the Information Bottleneck method by plotting the amount of information in the input data against the compressed representation. The claim that there is a causal link between information-theoretic compression and generalization, measured by mutual information, is plausible, but results from different studies are conflicting. In contrast to mutual information, TE can capture temporal relationships between variables. To explore such links, in our novel approach we use TE to quantify information transfer between neural layers and perform Information Plane analysis. We obtained encouraging experimental results, opening the possibility for further investigations.

papers.title: Transfer Entropy in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can Transfer Entropy be used to improve training efficiency and interpretability in deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Transfer Entropy can be used to improve training efficiency and interpretability in CNNs and GCNs, reducing training time and improving accuracy, and providing insights into information flow.
papers.conclusion: Transfer Entropy is a promising tool for improving deep learning models, but challenges such as computational overhead remain.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Entropy accelerates training in MLPs and CNNs, reducing the number of epochs needed.
Transfer Entropy improves accuracy in CNNs and GCNs.
Transfer Entropy helps mitigate oversmoothing in GCNs.
Transfer Entropy provides a way to analyze causal information flow in neural networks.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead and complexity of TE estimation for large networks.
TE does not provide full interpretability of neural network decisions.
future_direction: Developing scalable methods for TE computation.
Integrating TE with other interpretability frameworks.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the application of Transfer Entropy (TE) in deep neural networks as a tool to improve training efficiency and analyze causal information flow. TE is a measure of directed information transfer that captures nonlinear dependencies and temporal dynamics between system components. The study investigates the use of TE in optimizing learning in Convolutional Neural Networks and Graph Convolutional Neural Networks. We present case studies that demonstrate reduced training times and improved accuracy. In addition, we apply TE within the framework of the Information Bottleneck theory, providing an insight into the trade-off between compression and information preservation during the training of deep learning architectures. The results highlight TE’s potential for identifying causal features, improving explainability, and addressing challenges such as oversmoothing in Graph Convolutional Neural Networks. Although computational overhead and complexity pose challenges, the findings emphasize the role of TE in creating more efficient and interpretable neural models.

papers.title: TURBO: The Swiss Knife of Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle for explaining auto-encoding methods, and can a new framework (TURBO) provide a more comprehensive theoretical foundation that generalizes a wider range of models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the TURBO framework, a novel information-theoretic formulation that maximizes mutual information between two data representations, providing a unifying theoretical explanation for a broad family of auto-encoder models (including VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN) where the Information Bottleneck principle falls short.
papers.conclusion: The TURBO framework serves as a powerful and versatile theoretical tool that unifies a wide spectrum of auto-encoding models, offering a richer understanding of data representation and neural network structure beyond the limitations of the Information Bottleneck principle.
papers.key_findings:
The Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle has inherent limitations, particularly when data has multiple relevant representations or when the latent space is physically meaningful rather than a compressed virtual space.
The TURBO framework, based on maximizing mutual information in two directions (direct and reverse paths), generalizes and provides a rigorous interpretation for models like AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, and normalizing flows, which the IBN principle struggles to explain.
TURBO's loss function decomposes into reconstruction and distribution matching terms, allowing it to seamlessly handle paired, unpaired, and partially paired data scenarios.
Many well-known models (VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, Flows) are shown to be special cases of the TURBO framework, each corresponding to a specific subset of its loss terms.
The framework enables new applications, such as linking physically meaningful modalities (e.g., particle momenta to detector responses) and transcoding between different data representations.
papers.abstract: We present a novel information-theoretic framework, termed as TURBO, designed to systematically analyse and generalise auto-encoding methods. We start by examining the principles of information bottleneck and bottleneck-based networks in the auto-encoding setting and identifying their inherent limitations, which become more prominent for data with multiple relevant, physics-related representations. The TURBO framework is then introduced, providing a comprehensive derivation of its core concept consisting of the maximisation of mutual information between various data representations expressed in two directions reflecting the information flows. We illustrate that numerous prevalent neural network models are encompassed within this framework. The paper underscores the insufficiency of the information bottleneck concept in elucidating all such models, thereby establishing TURBO as a preferable theoretical reference. The introduction of TURBO contributes to a richer understanding of data representation and the structure of neural network models, enabling more efficient and versatile applications.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods.
