Examines single layers in isolation, not how relational structures compose across layers or whether hierarchy introduces or reduces ambiguity.
future_direction: Applying the framework to more complex scenarios: unsupervised or self-supervised learning, naturalistic datasets, recurrent networks with temporal dynamics, or deeper hierarchical architectures.
Analyzing functional connectivity patterns during actual stimulus processing, particularly in biological neural recordings.
Applying the framework to biological neural data to test if low representational ambiguity correlates with conscious perception.
papers.abstract: Representations pervade our daily experience, from letters representing sounds to bit strings encoding digital files. While such representations require externally defined decoders to convey meaning, conscious experience appears fundamentally different: a neural state corresponding to perceiving a red square cannot alternatively encode the experience of a green square. This intrinsic property of consciousness suggests that conscious representations must be unambiguous in a way that conventional representations are not. We formalize this intuition using information theory, defining representational ambiguity as the conditional entropy H(I|R) over possible interpretations I given a representation R. Through experiments on neural networks trained to classify MNIST digits, we demonstrate that relational structures in network connectivity can unambiguously encode representational content. Using both learned decoders and direct geometric matching, we achieve perfect (100%) accuracy for dropout-trained networks and 38% for standard backpropagation in identifying output neuron class identity, despite identical task performance, demonstrating that representational ambiguity can arise orthogonally to behavioral accuracy. We further show that spatial position information of input neurons can be decoded from network connectivity with R2 up to 0.844. These results provide a quantitative method for measuring representational ambiguity in neural systems and demonstrate that neural networks can exhibit the low-ambiguity representations posited as necessary (though not sufficient) by theoretical accounts of consciousness.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Quantifying information stored in synaptic connections rather than in firing patterns of neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the information encoded by synaptic connections in neural networks, as opposed to firing patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a theoretical framework to analytically derive the Shannon mutual information between data and ensembles of synaptic connections in a continuous Hopfield network, revealing synergistic interactions among synapses.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an interpretable framework for quantitatively understanding information storage in neural networks through synaptic connectivity, illustrating the duality of synaptic connectivity and neural population activity in learning and memory.
papers.key_findings:
The mutual information about a data pattern stored in a synaptic connection or ensemble decreases as the total number of stored patterns increases.
The mutual information encoded by an ensemble of synaptic connections increases with the number of connections in the ensemble, approximately scaling as n^1.1.
The information contributed per synaptic connection increases with ensemble size, while the variability of this contribution decreases, indicating synergy where the whole encodes more than the sum of its parts.
The framework corroborates the paradigm of distributed coding from the perspective of synaptic connections.
The analysis suggests a superlinear relationship between the number of storable patterns and network size (P ~ d^1.2) based on information in connectivity, differing from traditional capacity analyses based on retrieval dynamics.
papers.limitation:
The analytical framework relies on approximations, such as the Fenton-Wilkinson method for summing log-normals and the assumption of multivariate log-normal distributions for data patterns.
The framework is developed for continuous Hopfield networks; its applicability to other neural network architectures remains to be explored.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of neural networks beyond Hopfield networks.
Applying the framework to analyze more complex, real-world data distributions.
Investigating the implications of synaptic information synergy for learning algorithms and network design.
papers.abstract: A cornerstone of our understanding of both biological and artificial neural networks is that they store information in the strengths of connections among the constituent neurons. However, in contrast to the well-established theory for quantifying information encoded by the firing patterns of neural networks, little is known about quantifying information encoded by its synaptic connections. Here, we develop a theoretical framework using continuous Hopfield networks as an exemplar for associative neural networks, and data that follow mixtures of broadly applicable multivariate log-normal distributions. Specifically, we analytically derive the Shannon mutual information between the data and singletons, pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and arbitrary n-tuples of synaptic connections within the network. Our framework corroborates well-established insights about storage capacity of, and distributed coding by, neural firing patterns. Strikingly, it discovers synergistic interactions among synapses, revealing that the information encoded jointly by all the synapses exceeds the 'sum of its parts'. Taken together, this study introduces an interpretable framework for quantitatively understanding information storage in neural networks, one that illustrates the duality of synaptic connectivity and neural population activity in learning and memory.

papers.title: Reconstruction of Hidden Representation for Robust Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust approach to feature representation by analyzing properties of Auto-Encoder based algorithms and using corruption and reconstruction on both input and hidden representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Double Denoising Auto-Encoders (DDAEs), a new model that uses corruption and reconstruction on both input and hidden representation to learn invariant and robust feature representations, supported by theoretical analysis on the lower bound of reconstruction error and the robustness of hidden representation reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: DDAEs are an effective model for unsupervised representation learning, demonstrating superior performance over existing state-of-the-art models on multiple datasets by leveraging corruption and reconstruction on both input and hidden representation.
papers.key_findings:
The reconstruction error of the input in Auto-Encoder based algorithms has a lower bound, providing a guiding principle for reconstruction.
The necessary condition for the reconstruction of the input to reach the ideal state is that the reconstruction of hidden representation achieves its ideal condition.
Minimizing the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the hidden representation has a deficiency and may lead to worse local optima, while minimizing the reconstruction error of the hidden representation is more robust.
DDAEs outperform Denoising Auto-Encoders (DAEs) and Contractive Auto-Encoders (CAEs) in learning robust feature representations, especially in the presence of noise or inessential features.
DDAEs can be trained with two different pre-training strategies (combined or separate optimization of the objective function) and achieve state-of-the-art performance on various datasets.
future_direction: Designing useful constraints or other operations on the hidden representation to develop more efficient representation learning models.
papers.abstract: This article aims to develop a new and robust approach to feature representation. Motivated by the success of Auto-Encoders, we first theoretically analyze and summarize the general properties of all algorithms that are based on traditional Auto-Encoders: (1) The reconstruction error of the input cannot be lower than a lower bound, which can be viewed as a guiding principle for reconstructing the input. Additionally, when the input is corrupted with noises, the reconstruction error of the corrupted input also cannot be lower than a lower bound. (2) The reconstruction of a hidden representation achieving its ideal situation is the necessary condition for the reconstruction of the input to reach the ideal state. (3) Minimizing the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the hidden representation has a deficiency and may result in a much worse local optimum value. We believe that minimizing the reconstruction error of the hidden representation is more robust than minimizing the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the hidden representation. Based on the above analysis, we propose a new model termed Double Denoising Auto-Encoders (DDAEs), which uses corruption and reconstruction on both the input and the hidden representation. We demonstrate that the proposed model is highly flexible and extensible and has a potentially better capability to learn invariant and robust feature representations. We also show that our model is more robust than Denoising Auto-Encoders (DAEs) for dealing with noises or inessential features. Furthermore, we detail how to train DDAEs with two different pretraining methods by optimizing the objective function in a combined and separate manner, respectively. Comparative experiments illustrate that the proposed model is significantly better for representation learning than the state-of-the-art models.

papers.title: Information Bottleneck Analysis of Deep Neural Networks via Lossy Compression
papers.research_question: How can we perform Information Bottleneck analysis on general neural networks by overcoming the curse of dimensionality in mutual information estimation via lossy compression?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for Information Bottleneck analysis of general neural networks by using lossy compression to overcome the curse of dimensionality in mutual information estimation, enabling analysis of larger networks and revealing multiple compression/fitting phases during training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework enables Information Bottleneck analysis for larger neural networks by mitigating the curse of dimensionality through lossy compression, revealing new features in mutual information dynamics during training.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed compression-based mutual information estimator performs accurately on synthetic datasets with known mutual information.
Information plane analysis of a convolutional classifier on MNIST reveals multiple compression and fitting phases during training, which correspond to different learning regimes (accelerated, stationary, or decelerated loss drop).
The weighted Kozachenko-Leonenko entropy estimator, when combined with compression, outperforms other tested estimators and MINE on high-dimensional synthetic data.
Theoretical bounds are provided for mutual information estimation under lossy compression, showing that the method can track the true mutual information within the errors of the estimator and the compression bounds.
The method relies on the manifold hypothesis and uses autoencoders for compression, which can be applied to stochastic neural networks to estimate information flow.
papers.limitation: The method relies on the manifold hypothesis and may lose information during compression, as arbitrary amounts of information can be lost if the compression is not lossless.
future_direction: Using normalizing flows for lossless and information-preserving compression to improve the approach.
Applying the method to various large neural networks and performing corresponding information plane analysis.
papers.abstract: The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle offers an information-theoretic framework for analyzing the training process of deep neural networks (DNNs). Its essence lies in tracking the dynamics of two mutual information (MI) values: between the hidden layer output and the DNN input/target. According to the hypothesis put forth by Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby (2017), the training process consists of two distinct phases: fitting and compression. The latter phase is believed to account for the good generalization performance exhibited by DNNs. Due to the challenging nature of estimating MI between high-dimensional random vectors, this hypothesis was only partially verified for NNs of tiny sizes or specific types, such as quantized NNs. In this paper, we introduce a framework for conducting IB analysis of general NNs. Our approach leverages the stochastic NN method proposed by Goldfeld et al. (2019) and incorporates a compression step to overcome the obstacles associated with high dimensionality. In other words, we estimate the MI between the compressed representations of high-dimensional random vectors. The proposed method is supported by both theoretical and practical justifications. Notably, we demonstrate the accuracy of our estimator through synthetic experiments featuring predefined MI values and comparison with MINE (Belghazi et al., 2018). Finally, we perform IB analysis on a close-to-real-scale convolutional DNN, which reveals new features of the MI dynamics.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Mitigate Position Bias in Large Language Models via Scaling a Single Dimension
papers.research_question: How can position bias ('lost in the middle') in long-context language models be mitigated by identifying and scaling positional information present in specific hidden state channels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that positional information in hidden states (introduced by the causal mask) is a cause of position bias and introduces a method to mitigate this bias by identifying and scaling a single 'positional channel' in the hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Scaling positional hidden states is an effective and generalizable method for mitigating position bias in LLMs, requiring modification of only one channel and causing minimal side effects on the model's original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weight patterns in retrieval-related layers exhibit a U-shape that correlates with the 'lost in the middle' performance bias.
Positional information from the causal mask is stored in hidden states and affects position bias, independent of position embeddings.
Specific channels (positional channels) in the hidden states exhibit monotonic activation patterns with token position.
Scaling a single identified positional channel in the hidden states, specifically for the last token's attention computation, can significantly mitigate position bias.
The proposed method improves performance on long-context tasks (e.g., up to 15.2% on a 'lost in the middle' benchmark) with minimal impact on general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The method is applied only to the attention queried by the last token and to a selected range of middle layers, based on engineering experience.
The search algorithm for the optimal channel relies on heuristics (monotonicity, smoothness) and a small calibration dataset.
future_direction: Extend the scaling method to affect the attention of more tokens, not just the last token.
Automate the selection of the scaling factor and the range of layers to apply the scaling.
Explore the integration of the method with other position bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in various real-world scenarios due to their excellent generalization capabilities and robust generative abilities. However, they exhibit position bias, also known as "lost in the middle", a phenomenon that is especially pronounced in long-context scenarios, which indicates the placement of the key information in different positions of a prompt can significantly affect accuracy. This paper first explores the micro-level manifestations of position bias, concluding that attention weights are a micro-level expression of position bias. It further identifies that, in addition to position embeddings, causal attention mask also contributes to position bias by creating position-specific hidden states. Based on these insights, we propose a method to mitigate position bias by scaling this positional hidden states. Experiments on the NaturalQuestions Multi-document QA, KV retrieval, LongBench and timeline reorder tasks, using various models including RoPE models, context windowextended models, and Alibi models, demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach. Our method can improve performance by up to 15.2% by modifying just one dimension of hidden states. Our code is available at https://aka.ms/PositionalHidden.

papers.title: Examining the causal structures of deep neural networks using information theory
papers.research_question: How can we quantify and track the causal structure of deep neural networks during training, and how does this relate to generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces effective information (EI) and its decomposition into sensitivity and degeneracy to quantify the causal structure of deep neural networks, enabling visualization of layer dynamics in a 'causal plane' and providing tools to understand generalization.
papers.conclusion: The introduced information-theoretic metrics provide a new way to analyze the causal structure of DNNs, which may help explain generalization and open up possibilities for future extensions to other network architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Effective information (EI) changes during training, with the largest changes occurring during the steepest reductions in loss.
The causal structure of a DNN differentiates according to task complexity, with MNIST-trained networks showing more differentiation in the causal plane than Iris-trained networks.
Redundant layers that do not contribute to the network's causal structure cluster along the EI nullcline and move little during training.
EI can be decomposed into sensitivity (strength of causal relationships in isolation) and degeneracy (overlap of edge weights), defining a causal plane for visualizing layer dynamics.
A measure of feedforward integrated information (φ_feedforward) shows higher values for more complex tasks, indicating greater joint effects in layer connectivity.
papers.limitation:
Computation of EI requires many noise samples for convergence, especially for wider network layers.
The measure of feedforward integrated information (φ_feedforward) is not bounded by zero and can be negative.
future_direction: Extend the method to other activation functions, unsupervised tasks, recurrent neural networks, and convolutional neural networks.
Assess decompositions and expansions of EI, such as integrated information of DNNs.
Direct measurement of individual instances of causation in DNNs.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are often examined at the level of their response to input, such as analyzing the mutual information between nodes and data sets. Yet DNNs can also be examined at the level of causation, exploring "what does what" within the layers of the network itself. Historically, analyzing the causal structure of DNNs has received less attention than understanding their responses to input. Yet definitionally, generalizability must be a function of a DNN's causal structure since it reflects how the DNN responds to unseen or even not-yet-defined future inputs. Here, we introduce a suite of metrics based on information theory to quantify and track changes in the causal structure of DNNs during training. Specifically, we introduce the effective information (EI) of a feedforward DNN, which is the mutual information between layer input and output following a maximum-entropy perturbation. The EI can be used to assess the degree of causal influence nodes and edges have over their downstream targets in each layer. We show that the EI can be further decomposed in order to examine the sensitivity of a layer (measured by how well edges transmit perturbations) and the degeneracy of a layer (measured by how edge overlap interferes with transmission), along with estimates of the amount of integrated information of a layer. Together, these properties define where each layer lies in the "causal plane" which can be used to visualize how layer connectivity becomes more sensitive or degenerate over time, and how integration changes during training, revealing how the layer-by-layer causal structure differentiates. These results may help in understanding the generalization capabilities of DNNs and provide foundational tools for making DNNs both more generalizable and more explainable.

papers.title: Emergence of Invariance and Disentanglement in Deep Representations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how invariance and disentanglement emerge in deep neural networks, and establishes connections between information in the weights, invariance, disentanglement, and generalization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that invariance and disentanglement in deep representations emerge from minimizing the information in the weights, and proposes a novel Information Bottleneck for the weights that controls this information and leads to better generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariance and disentanglement in deep representations emerge from minimizing the information in the weights, and that regularizing this information leads to better generalization and predictable phase transitions.
papers.key_findings:
Invariance to nuisance factors in a deep neural network is equivalent to information minimality of the learned representation.
Stacking layers and injecting noise during training naturally bias the network towards learning invariant representations.
The information in the weights bounds the information in the representation and its total correlation, linking weight complexity to invariance and disentanglement.
Regularizing the information in the weights leads to a sharp phase transition between overfitting and underfitting when training on random labels, as predicted by theory.
Flat minima of the loss correspond to low information in the weights, connecting the geometry of the loss to generalization.
papers.limitation:
The use of a log-uniform prior leads to a vacuous generalization bound because it is an improper prior.
Computing the nuclear norm of the Hessian is computationally expensive.
The theory treats the dataset as random, but in practice we only have one fixed dataset.
future_direction: Measuring the distance between tasks, as opposed to distance between distributions.
papers.abstract: Using established principles from Information Theory and Statistics, we show that in a deep neural network invariance to nuisance factors is equivalent to information minimality of the learned representation, and that stacking layers and injecting noise during training naturally bias the network towards learning invariant representations. We then show that, in order to avoid memorization, we need to limit the quantity of information stored in the weights, which leads to a novel usage of the Information Bottleneck Lagrangian on the weights as a learning criterion. This also has an alternative interpretation as minimizing a PAC-Bayesian bound on the test error. Finally, we exploit a duality between weights and activations induced by the architecture, to show that the information in the weights bounds the minimality and Total Correlation of the layers, therefore showing that regularizing the weights explicitly or implicitly, using SGD, not only helps avoid overfitting, but also fosters invariance and disentangling of the learned representation. The theory also enables predicting sharp phase transitions between underfitting and overfitting random labels at precise information values, and sheds light on the relation between the geometry of the loss function, in particular so-called “flat minima,” and generalization.

papers.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the hidden states in models of different scales? The paper investigates whether there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models trained on similar data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Linear Representation Transferability (LRT) Hypothesis and provides empirical evidence that affine mappings between hidden states of different-sized models can transfer steering vectors, enabling small models to steer large models.
papers.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence for the LRT hypothesis, suggesting that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the hypothesis is a promising direction for understanding representation alignment across model scales.
papers.key_findings:
Affine mappings can be learned between the hidden states of small and large models from the same family.
Steering vectors learned on small models retain their semantic effect when transferred to large models via the learned affine map.
The transferred steering vectors are as effective as those learned directly on the large model for tasks like refusal behavior removal and logit-based evaluation.
The feature spaces of models, as represented by sparse autoencoder decoder matrices, are approximately linearly related.
The conceptual framework of a universal representation space provides a plausible explanation for the linear transferability.
papers.limitation:
The limits of transferability across very different model sizes (e.g., 100M to 70B) are not yet understood.
Transferability across different model families or architectures is challenging due to differences in tokenization schemes and architectural design.
future_direction: Investigating the limits of transferability across model sizes.
Exploring transferability across different model families and architectures.
Developing theoretical foundations for the LRT hypothesis and the universal representation space.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that neural networks with similar architectures trained on similar data learn shared representations relevant to the learning task. We build on this idea by extending the conceptual framework where representations learned across models trained on the same data can be expressed as linear combinations of a \emph{universal} set of basis features. These basis features underlie the learning task itself and remain consistent across models, regardless of scale. From this framework, we propose the \textbf{Linear Representation Transferability (LRT)} Hypothesis -- that there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models. To test this hypothesis, we learn affine mappings between the hidden states of models of different sizes and evaluate whether steering vectors -- directions in hidden state space associated with specific model behaviors -- retain their semantic effect when transferred from small to large language models using the learned mappings. We find strong empirical evidence that such affine mappings can preserve steering behaviors. These findings suggest that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the LRT hypothesis may be a promising direction on understanding representation alignment across model scales.

papers.title: Layerwise Change of Knowledge in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does a deep neural network gradually extract new knowledge and forget noisy features through layers during forward propagation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the definition of interactions to intermediate layers of DNNs, enabling the tracking of newly emerged and forgotten interactions through layers, and relates these changes to generalization capacity.
papers.conclusion: The paper uses interaction primitives to represent knowledge encoded by DNNs and tracks their layer-wise change, revealing changes in generalization capacity and feature instability.
papers.key_findings:
Early and middle layers fit target interactions but encode redundant interactions, while later layers remove such redundant interactions.
Low-order interactions have stronger generalization capacity than high-order interactions.
Low-order interactions are more stable to input noise than high-order interactions.
The layer-wise change of interactions reveals changes in representation complexity and generalization capacity.
papers.limitation: Aligning a DNN's inference logic (interaction primitives) with human cognition remains a challenge.
future_direction: using interaction primitives to represent the complex learning dynamics of a DNN
identifying and boosting the reliable/generalizable interaction primitives
aligning a DNN's detailed inference logic (interaction primitives) with human cognition
papers.abstract: This paper aims to explain how a deep neural network (DNN) gradually extracts new knowledge and forgets noisy features through layers in forward propagation. Up to now, although the definition of knowledge encoded by the DNN has not reached a consensus, Previous studies have derived a series of mathematical evidence to take interactions as symbolic primitive inference patterns encoded by a DNN. We extend the definition of interactions and, for the first time, extract interactions encoded by intermediate layers. We quantify and track the newly emerged interactions and the forgotten interactions in each layer during the forward propagation, which shed new light on the learning behavior of DNNs. The layer-wise change of interactions also reveals the change of the generalization capacity and instability of feature representations of a DNN.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do disentangled representations emerge in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-task learning in evidence accumulation tasks leads to disentangled representations in the latent state of autoregressive models, with theoretical guarantees on emergence conditions.
papers.conclusion: Multi-task learning establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, explaining their generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical guarantees show that any optimal multi-task classifier must encode a maximum likelihood estimate of the ground truth in its latent state, leading to abstract and disentangled representations as the number of tasks increases.
RNNs trained on multi-task classification learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, enabling zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization.
Transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, achieving orthogonality even with fewer tasks compared to RNNs.
Noise in observations is necessary for disentangled representations to emerge, as it prevents saturation and preserves distance information.
The framework is robust to various manipulations including correlated inputs, non-linear decision boundaries, and free reaction-time tasks.
future_direction: Characterizing representation learning with multiple manifold decision boundaries
Exploring interplay between task diversity, energy constraints, and the emergence of shared representations
papers.abstract: Intelligent perception and interaction with the world hinges on internal representations that capture its underlying structure (''disentangled'' or ''abstract'' representations). Disentangled representations serve as world models, isolating latent factors of variation in the world along approximately orthogonal directions, thus facilitating feature-based generalization. We provide experimental and theoretical results guaranteeing the emergence of disentangled representations in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks, canonical in the neuroscience literature. The key conceptual finding is that, by producing accurate multi-task classification estimates, a system implicitly represents a set of coordinates specifying a disentangled representation of the underlying latent state of the data it receives. The theory provides conditions for the emergence of these representations in terms of noise, number of tasks, and evidence accumulation time. We experimentally validate these predictions in RNNs trained to multi-task, which learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, leading to zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in predicting latent factors. We demonstrate the robustness of our framework across autoregressive architectures, decision boundary geometries and in tasks requiring classification confidence estimation. We find that transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, which might explain their unique world understanding abilities. Overall, our framework establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, and helps explain why ANNs often arrive at human-interpretable concepts, and how they both may acquire exceptional zero-shot generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Under the Hood of Neural Networks: Characterizing Learned Representations by Functional Neuron Populations and Network Ablations
papers.research_question: What are the roles of single neurons and groups of neurons within a neural network in fulfilling a learned task? How can learned representations be characterized by activation patterns and network ablations to reveal functional neuron populations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper characterizes learned representations in neural networks by identifying functional neuron populations through activation patterns and network ablations, showing that a neuron's activation magnitude, selectivity, and impact on performance are insufficient stand-alone indicators for its importance.
papers.conclusion: Understanding how knowledge is represented and localized in artificial networks is beneficial for advancing transfer learning and for providing measures for large-scale studies in neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Learned representations evolve to become more distinct along network layers, improving class separation in the activation-space.
Network ablations distort the activation-space, leading to misclassifications, but the relative positions of units are mostly preserved, suggesting a holistic effect.
Functional neuron populations exist: groups of neurons that jointly activate in response to specific stimuli or have a similar impact on network accuracy when ablated.
The size of functional neuron populations varies greatly across classes, indicating different network capacity usage per class.
No single metric (activation magnitude, selectivity, or ablation impact) sufficiently describes the role of a single unit within the whole network.
papers.limitation:
The number of samples (10 classes) is small, limiting the descriptive statistical power of the correlation tests.
Investigating the effect of single unit ablations does not allow determining whether the ablated unit is singly important or part of an important path through the network that has been altered.
future_direction: Determine how robustness of class-specific representations against network ablations can be characterized and achieved purposefully.
Identify important paths along the network, rather than just single units, to understand the flow of information.
Investigate how the localization of a class-specific representation is affected by class-specific properties and how the robustness of these representations depends on these properties.
papers.abstract: The need for more transparency of the decision-making processes in artificial neural networks steadily increases driven by their applications in safety critical and ethically challenging domains such as autonomous driving or medical diagnostics. We address today's lack of transparency of neural networks and shed light on the roles of single neurons and groups of neurons within the network fulfilling a learned task. Inspired by research in the field of neuroscience, we characterize the learned representations by activation patterns and network ablations, revealing functional neuron populations that a) act jointly in response to specific stimuli or b) have similar impact on the network's performance after being ablated. We find that neither a neuron's magnitude or selectivity of activation, nor its impact on network performance are sufficient stand-alone indicators for its importance for the overall task. We argue that such indicators are essential for future advances in transfer learning and modern neuroscience.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: On the Transferability of Representations in Neural Networks Between\n Datasets and Tasks
papers.research_question: How do representations in deep networks transfer between different datasets and tasks, and what factors influence this transferability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks is non-symmetric, influenced more by dataset nature than network architecture, and can serve as a proxy for task relatedness.
papers.conclusion: The observations highlight the importance of curriculum methods and structured approaches to designing systems for multiple tasks to maximize knowledge transfer and minimize interference between datasets or tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise transferability between datasets can be non-symmetric, e.g., features from CIFAR datasets are more transferable to SVHN than vice versa.
The nature of the datasets or tasks involved is more influential on transferability compared to the neural network architecture.
Initial layers in deep networks are more transferable than final layers across different tasks.
Layer-wise transferability can be used as a proxy for quantifying task relatedness.
Representations learned on more general classes (e.g., CIFAR) are more transferable than those learned on specific classes (e.g., SVHN digits).
papers.abstract:
Deep networks, composed of multiple layers of hierarchical distributed
representations, tend to learn low-level features in initial layers and
transition to high-level features towards final layers. Paradigms such as
transfer learning, multi-task learning, and continual learning leverage this
notion of generic hierarchical distributed representations to share knowledge
across datasets and tasks. Herein, we study the layer-wise transferability of
representations in deep networks across a few datasets and tasks and note some
interesting empirical observations.

papers.title: Disentangled Representations in Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations in neural models that are interpretable, reusable, and performant, without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods (DC-IGN and CFN) for learning disentangled representations in graphics and computation, which are interpretable, reusable, and performant without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled representations are valuable for interpretability and reuse, and the proposed methods (DC-IGN and CFN) are effective in learning such representations in the domains of graphics and computation.
papers.key_findings:
DC-IGN can learn a disentangled graphics code for 3D faces and chairs, enabling novel view synthesis and re-rendering under different lighting and pose conditions.
CFN can disentangle computational tasks, factorize a multitask learning problem, and is practically immune to catastrophic forgetting.
Explicit disentanglement training is critical for novel-view reconstruction compared to entangled representations.
The decoder in DC-IGN can function as a 3D rendering engine, indicating a truly disentangled representation.
CFN achieves disentanglement with no performance penalty and with fewer parameters than a traditional feedforward network.
papers.limitation:
The current formulation of SGVB is restricted to continuous latent variables, but real-world scenes may require discrete distributions.
Scaling to more complex scenes may require deeper architectures.
The decoder network might be replaced by a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained model-based inference.
future_direction: Experiment with deeper architectures to handle more complex scenes and object categories.
Extend the model to handle discrete distributions or to a recurrent setting.
Use importance-weighted autoencoders to capture more complex probabilistic structure.
Replace the decoder with a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained inference.
Explore multi-step CFN for deeper computations and curricula.
Investigate non-differentiable functions in CFN and hierarchical computation.
Unify the two approaches for unsupervised inference of factors of variation in videos.
papers.abstract: Representation learning is the foundation for the recent success of neural network models. However, the distributed representations generated by neural networks are far from ideal. Due to their highly entangled nature, they are di cult to reuse and interpret, and they do a poor job of capturing the sparsity which is present in real- world transformations. In this paper, I describe methods for learning disentangled representations in the two domains of graphics and computation. These methods allow neural methods to learn representations which are easy to interpret and reuse, yet they incur little or no penalty to performance. In the Graphics section, I demonstrate the ability of these methods to infer the generating parameters of images and rerender those images under novel conditions. In the Computation section, I describe a model which is able to factorize a multitask learning problem into subtasks and which experiences no catastrophic forgetting. Together these techniques provide the tools to design a wide range of models that learn disentangled representations and better model the factors of variation in the real world.

papers.title: Theory of the superposition principle for randomized connectionist\n representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: What is the retrieval accuracy and information capacity of superposition operations in neural networks, and how can recency effects be incorporated to avoid catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: A theory for superposition operations in neural networks is presented, showing that networks can achieve a channel capacity of about half a bit per neuron, and novel models with recency effects are proposed to avoid catastrophic forgetting for infinite data streams.
papers.conclusion: The theory enables neural networks based on VSAs to be appropriately scaled and optimized to handle communication or memory demands.
papers.key_findings:
The theory maps VSA models to linear RNNs and derives a single equation for retrieval accuracy.
Networks representing information in superposition can achieve a channel capacity of about half a bit per neuron.
Superposition operations with recency effects are proposed to avoid catastrophic forgetting when representing the history of infinite data streams.
The theory accurately predicts simulation experiments and explains why many VSA models exhibit the same retrieval accuracy and capacity.
A recurrent neural network optimized by learning does not exceed the performance of existing VSA models.
papers.abstract:
To understand cognitive reasoning in the brain, it has been proposed that
symbols and compositions of symbols are represented by activity patterns
(vectors) in a large population of neurons. Formal models implementing this
idea [Plate 2003], [Kanerva 2009], [Gayler 2003], [Eliasmith 2012] include a
reversible superposition operation for representing with a single vector an
entire set of symbols or an ordered sequence of symbols. If the representation
space is high-dimensional, large sets of symbols can be superposed and
individually retrieved. However, crosstalk noise limits the accuracy of
retrieval and information capacity. To understand information processing in the
brain and to design artificial neural systems for cognitive reasoning, a theory
of this superposition operation is essential. Here, such a theory is presented.
The superposition operations in different existing models are mapped to linear
neural networks with unitary recurrent matrices, in which retrieval accuracy
can be analyzed by a single equation. We show that networks representing
information in superposition can achieve a channel capacity of about half a bit
per neuron, a significant fraction of the total available entropy. Going beyond
existing models, superposition operations with recency effects are proposed
that avoid catastrophic forgetting when representing the history of infinite
data streams. These novel models correspond to recurrent networks with
non-unitary matrices or with nonlinear neurons, and can be analyzed and
optimized with an extension of our theory.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: Superposition as Lossy Compression: Measure with Sparse Autoencoders and Connect to Adversarial Vulnerability
papers.research_question: How can superposition in neural networks be measured, and does superposition cause adversarial vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents an information-theoretic framework to measure superposition in neural networks using sparse autoencoders, and finds that adversarial training does not universally reduce superposition; its effect depends on task complexity and network capacity.
papers.conclusion: Superposition can be measured as lossy compression, and its relationship with adversarial vulnerability is nuanced, with adversarial training leading to feature expansion in low-complexity/high-capacity settings and feature reduction in high-complexity/low-capacity settings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed superposition measure (ψ) strongly correlates with ground truth in toy models (r=0.94).
Dropout systematically reduces effective features and superposition.
Algorithmic tasks (e.g., multi-task sparse parity) show minimal superposition (ψ ≤ 1).
During grokking, a sharp drop in superposition occurs at the generalization transition.
Adversarial training can increase or decrease superposition depending on task complexity and network capacity, revealing abundance and scarcity regimes.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes SAE dictionary elements correspond one-to-one with genuine computational features, which can fail due to feature splitting, merging, or ghost features.
The linear representation assumption may be violated by hierarchical structure, gating mechanisms, or combinatorial feature interactions.
The magnitude-importance correspondence (|zi| reflects feature importance) may break if SAE reconstruction preserves irrelevant details or if feature importance is context-dependent.
The independent information assumption (Shannon entropy correctly aggregates information) fails when features are correlated, synergistic, or redundantly encoded.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures and tasks.
Further investigate the connection between superposition and robustness.
Explore the implications for interpretability and adversarial defense.
papers.abstract: Neural networks achieve remarkable performance through superposition: encoding multiple features as overlapping directions in activation space rather than dedicating individual neurons to each feature. This challenges interpretability, yet we lack principled methods to measure superposition. We present an information-theoretic framework measuring a neural representation's effective degrees of freedom. We apply Shannon entropy to sparse autoencoder activations to compute the number of effective features as the minimum neurons needed for interference-free encoding. Equivalently, this measures how many "virtual neurons" the network simulates through superposition. When networks encode more effective features than actual neurons, they must accept interference as the price of compression. Our metric strongly correlates with ground truth in toy models, detects minimal superposition in algorithmic tasks, and reveals systematic reduction under dropout. Layer-wise patterns mirror intrinsic dimensionality studies on Pythia-70M. The metric also captures developmental dynamics, detecting sharp feature consolidation during grokking. Surprisingly, adversarial training can increase effective features while improving robustness, contradicting the hypothesis that superposition causes vulnerability. Instead, the effect depends on task complexity and network capacity: simple tasks with ample capacity allow feature expansion (abundance regime), while complex tasks or limited capacity force reduction (scarcity regime). By defining superposition as lossy compression, this work enables principled measurement of how neural networks organize information under computational constraints, connecting superposition to adversarial robustness.

papers.title: Adaptive Estimators Show Information Compression in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks with non-saturating activation functions compress information during training, and how do different activation functions and regularization affect compression?
papers.core_contribution: Developed adaptive mutual information estimators (EBAB and aKDE) and used them to show that compression occurs in networks with non-saturating activation functions, that L2 regularization induces compression, and that only compression in the last layer correlates with generalization.
papers.conclusion: Compression is not restricted to saturating activation functions; L2 regularization induces compression; and generalization accuracy is positively correlated with compression only in the last layer, not in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Adaptive mutual information estimators (EBAB and aKDE) enable more sensitive measurement of compression in networks with unbounded activation functions.
Compression is not restricted to saturating activation functions; it occurs in some non-saturating functions (e.g., ELU, Swish, centered softplus) and varies with initialization.
L2 regularization induces compression and clusters the mutual information of all layers to a single point on the information plane.
Compression in the last (softmax) layer is positively correlated with generalization, but compression in hidden layers is not.
There is large variation in compression between different network initializations.
papers.limitation:
The networks explored were much smaller and more straightforward than many state-of-the-art networks used for practical applications.
The methods for computing information, although adaptive for any distribution of network activity, were not rigorously derived.
The compression metric is ad-hoc.
future_direction: Experiments with larger convolutional neural networks could be used to explore the possibility that compression behavior is affected by network size.
Further work is needed to understand the other factors contributing to compression.
Further research could optimize regularization to stabilize layers on the information bottleneck bound for better generalization and link information compression to memorization.
papers.abstract: To improve how neural networks function it is crucial to understand their learning process. The information bottleneck theory of deep learning proposes that neural networks achieve good generalization by compressing their representations to disregard information that is not relevant to the task. However, empirical evidence for this theory is conflicting, as compression was only observed when networks used saturating activation functions. In contrast, networks with non-saturating activation functions achieved comparable levels of task performance but did not show compression. In this paper we developed more robust mutual information estimation techniques, that adapt to hidden activity of neural networks and produce more sensitive measurements of activations from all functions, especially unbounded functions. Using these adaptive estimation techniques, we explored compression in networks with a range of different activation functions. With two improved methods of estimation, firstly, we show that saturation of the activation function is not required for compression, and the amount of compression varies between different activation functions. We also find that there is a large amount of variation in compression between different network initializations. Secondary, we see that L2 regularization leads to significantly increased compression, while preventing overfitting. Finally, we show that only compression of the last layer is positively correlated with generalization.

papers.title: Collective variables of neural networks: empirical time evolution and scaling laws
papers.research_question: How can the entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) be used to understand learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel as collective variables to analyze neural network training dynamics, identifying two learning regimes (information compression and structure formation) and showing that structure formation characterizes the deep learning regime.
papers.conclusion: Entropy and trace of the NTK provide a universal framework for understanding neural network learning dynamics and scaling, with structure formation identified as a hallmark of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy of the NTK reveals two learning regimes: information compression (entropy decreases) where gradient vectors align, and structure formation (entropy increases) where the network separates data to create richer representations.
Small networks tend to remain in the compression regime with limited performance, while large networks transition to structure formation, which is associated with improved performance and defines a deep learning regime.
The trace of the NTK, representing an effective learning rate, increases during training, indicating growing network sensitivity to new data and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks or benefits for continual learning.
The dynamics observed via entropy and trace are universal across diverse architectures including transformers, GNNs, CNNs, and reinforcement learning agents.
Architecture scaling (width and depth) influences the entropy and trace, with deeper networks showing reduced entropy at initialization but capable of achieving higher entropy after training when sufficiently wide.
future_direction: Explore how scaling behavior for different activation functions can be used for targeted architecture selection.
Investigate the trace property to reduce model sensitivity and improve continual learning strategies.
Explore avenues for improved stability by reducing trace late in training.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel means for understanding learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks. We show that certain measures on the spectrum of the empirical neural tangent kernel, specifically entropy and trace, yield insight into the representations learned by a neural network and how these can be improved through architecture scaling. These results are demonstrated first on test cases before being shown on more complex networks, including transformers, auto-encoders, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning studies. In testing on a wide range of architectures, we highlight the universal nature of training dynamics and further discuss how it can be used to understand the mechanisms behind learning in neural networks. We identify two such dominant mechanisms present throughout machine learning training. The first, information compression, is seen through a reduction in the entropy of the NTK spectrum during training, and occurs predominantly in small neural networks. The second, coined structure formation, is seen through an increasing entropy and thus, the creation of structure in the neural network representations beyond the prior established by the network at initialization. Due to the ubiquity of the latter in deep neural network architectures and its flexibility in the creation of feature-rich representations, we argue that this form of evolution of the network's entropy be considered the onset of a deep learning regime.

papers.title: What Information Does a ResNet Compress?
papers.research_question: Does the information bottleneck principle apply to a realistic setting using a larger and deeper convolutional architecture (ResNet) trained on realistic images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that ResNets exhibit information compression in hidden layers during training for both classification and autoencoding tasks, and provides a method using decoder models to visualize what information is kept and discarded.
papers.conclusion: ResNets exhibit information compression during training, and the proposed experimental framework allows for an intuitive visualization of the type of information that is compressed.
papers.key_findings:
Two stages of learning (fitting and compression) are observed for both classification and autoencoding.
Compression occurs in hidden layers even for autoencoding, where the target is identical to the input.
Conditionally generated images from PixelCNN++ decoders show the network learns to discard class-irrelevant information (e.g., background color) while retaining class-relevant information.
The initial fitting phase is longer (5-10 epochs) than previously suggested and may have a larger influence on the solution.
The method enables visualization of class invariances learned by the network.
papers.limitation:
The tightness of the lower bound on mutual information depends on the quality of the decoder model, and an ablation study on this is left for future work.
Training the PixelCNN++ decoder models is computationally expensive, taking approximately 15 days per run on a single GPU.
future_direction: Future work could design models that target the invariances learned by ResNets, as illustrated by the conditional samples.
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck principle (Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby, 2017) suggests that SGD-based training of deep neural networks results in optimally compressed hidden layers, from an information theoretic perspective. However, this claim was established on toy data.
