The goal of the work we present here is to test whether the information bottleneck principle is applicable to a realistic setting using a larger and deeper convolutional architecture, a ResNet model. We trained PixelCNN++ models as inverse representation decoders to measure the mutual information between hidden layers of a ResNet and input image data, when trained for (1) classification and (2) autoencoding. We find that two stages of learning happen for both training regimes, and that compression does occur, even for an autoencoder. Sampling images by conditioning on hidden layers' activations offers an intuitive visualisation to understand what a ResNets learns to forget.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Take Care of Your Prompt Bias! Investigating and Mitigating Prompt Bias in Factual Knowledge Extraction
papers.research_question: How does prompt bias affect the reliability of factual knowledge extraction benchmarks, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates prompt bias in factual knowledge extraction and proposes a representation-based debiasing approach that removes biased components from model representations, improving benchmark reliability and retrieval performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that prompt bias is a significant issue in factual knowledge extraction and that the proposed debiasing approach effectively mitigates it, leading to more reliable benchmarks and improved retrieval performance.
papers.key_findings:
All prompts exhibit non-negligible bias, with gradient-based prompts (AutoPrompt, OptiPrompt) showing significantly higher bias.
Prompt bias can overfit imbalanced datasets like LAMA, inflating benchmark accuracy unreasonably.
Prompt bias can mislead language models, causing incorrect predictions and impairing retrieval capability.
The proposed debiasing approach rectifies overfitted performance and improves prompt retrieval capability (up to 10% absolute gain).
After debiasing, the knowledge retrieval abilities of manual prompts are comparable to state-of-the-art prompts, suggesting that complex prompts achieve performance mainly through overfitting.
papers.limitation:
The debiasing method is a preliminary exploration and can be further improved.
The prompt bias estimation strategy (by masking the input information) may be suboptimal.
future_direction: Explore the bias and effectiveness of the method in other models and tasks (e.g., GLUE, SuperGLUE).
Improve the debiasing method and prompt bias estimation strategies.
Evaluate prompts with the debiasing method when seeking better retrieval capability.
papers.abstract: Recent research shows that pre-trained language models (PLMs) suffer from "prompt bias" in factual knowledge extraction, i.e., prompts tend to introduce biases toward specific labels. Prompt bias presents a significant challenge in assessing the factual knowledge within PLMs. Therefore, this paper aims to improve the reliability of existing benchmarks by thoroughly investigating and mitigating prompt bias. We show that: 1) all prompts in the experiments exhibit non-negligible bias, with gradient-based prompts like AutoPrompt and OptiPrompt displaying significantly higher levels of bias; 2) prompt bias can amplify benchmark accuracy unreasonably by overfitting the test datasets, especially on imbalanced datasets like LAMA. Based on these findings, we propose a representation-based approach to mitigate the prompt bias during inference time. Specifically, we first estimate the biased representation using prompt-only querying, and then remove it from the model's internal representations to generate the debiased representations, which are used to produce the final debiased outputs. Experiments across various prompts, PLMs, and benchmarks show that our approach can not only correct the overfitted performance caused by prompt bias, but also significantly improve the prompt retrieval capability (up to 10% absolute performance gain). These results indicate that our approach effectively alleviates prompt bias in knowledge evaluation, thereby enhancing the reliability of benchmark assessments. Hopefully, our plug-and-play approach can be a golden standard to strengthen PLMs toward reliable knowledge bases. Code and data are released in https://github.com/FelliYang/PromptBias.

papers.title: Hamiltonian Mechanics of Feature Learning: Bottleneck Structure in Leaky ResNets
papers.research_question: How does feature learning occur in Leaky ResNets, and what explains the emergence of bottleneck structure in deep networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hamiltonian reformulation of Leaky ResNets that decomposes the dynamics into kinetic and potential energies, providing an intuitive understanding of feature learning and explaining the emergence of bottleneck structure for large effective depths.
papers.conclusion: The Hamiltonian mechanics framework offers an intuitive understanding of feature learning in ResNets, highlighting the balance between kinetic and potential energies and explaining the bottleneck structure as a result of separation of timescales for large effective depths.
papers.key_findings:
For large effective depths, the potential energy (cost of identity) dominates, leading to a separation of timescales where representations rapidly jump to a low-dimensional bottleneck, move slowly within it, and then jump back to high-dimensional outputs.
The Hamiltonian is constant along the representation path and can be decomposed into kinetic and potential energies, balancing path length and low-dimensional representations.
The cost of identity measures the dimensionality of representations and is minimized at stable non-negative representations.
An adaptive layer step-size discretization scheme can improve test performance by adapting to the separation of timescales.
papers.abstract: We study Leaky ResNets, which interpolate between ResNets and Fully-Connected nets depending on an 'effective depth' hyper-parameter $\tilde{L}$. In the infinite depth limit, we study 'representation geodesics' $A_{p}$: continuous paths in representation space (similar to NeuralODEs) from input $p=0$ to output $p=1$ that minimize the parameter norm of the network. We give a Lagrangian and Hamiltonian reformulation, which highlight the importance of two terms: a kinetic energy which favors small layer derivatives $\partial_{p}A_{p}$ and a potential energy that favors low-dimensional representations, as measured by the 'Cost of Identity'. The balance between these two forces offers an intuitive understanding of feature learning in ResNets. We leverage this intuition to explain the emergence of a bottleneck structure, as observed in previous work: for large $\tilde{L}$ the potential energy dominates and leads to a separation of timescales, where the representation jumps rapidly from the high dimensional inputs to a low-dimensional representation, move slowly inside the space of low-dimensional representations, before jumping back to the potentially high-dimensional outputs. Inspired by this phenomenon, we train with an adaptive layer step-size to adapt to the separation of timescales.

papers.title: Understanding and Leveraging the Learning Phases of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the learning dynamics of neural networks, specifically the existence of phases in reconstruction loss during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper empirically and theoretically demonstrates the existence of three phases in reconstruction loss during neural network training (near constant, decrease, increase) and shows that for transfer learning, pre-training should stop before optimal performance on the pre-training task.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights the existence of multiple phases in reconstruction loss during learning, providing insight that can be used to improve transfer learning via early stopping in pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical evidence shows three phases in reconstruction loss: near constant, decrease, and increase during training.
Theoretical proof for the existence of these phases in a single-layer linear classifier with a derived data model.
Reconstruction loss is minimal when the classifier is not yet fully optimized, indicating a trade-off between discriminative performance and input information retention.
For transfer learning, stopping pre-training early (when reconstruction loss is minimal) improves downstream task performance.
The phases are most pronounced in the last layers of the network, where features become more discriminative.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions about the data model and shallow networks (single dense layer and softmax layer).
The phases are most notable for the last layers of a network.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper networks.
Investigating the prevalence of these phases in other architectures like RNNs and transformers.
papers.abstract: The learning dynamics of deep neural networks are not well understood. The information bottleneck (IB) theory proclaimed separate fitting and compression phases. But they have since been heavily debated. We comprehensively analyze the learning dynamics by investigating a layer's reconstruction ability of the input and prediction performance based on the evolution of parameters during training. We empirically show the existence of three phases using common datasets and architectures such as ResNet and VGG: (i) near constant reconstruction loss, (ii) decrease, and (iii) increase. We also derive an empirically grounded data model and prove the existence of phases for single-layer networks. Technically, our approach leverages classical complexity analysis. It differs from IB by relying on measuring reconstruction loss rather than information theoretic measures to relate information of intermediate layers and inputs. Our work implies a new best practice for transfer learning: We show empirically that the pre-training of a classifier should stop well before its performance is optimal.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: Information Bottleneck in Deep Learning - A Semiotic Approach
papers.research_question: What is the connection between the information bottleneck principle and semiotic superization in CNNs, and can the evolution of spatial entropy in saliency maps be used to design a layer-wise early stopping criterion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a link between the information bottleneck principle and semiotic superization via the evolution of spatial entropy in CNN saliency maps, and introduces a heuristic layer-wise early stopping training strategy based on entropy variability.
papers.conclusion: There is a connection between the evolution of spatial entropy of saliency maps and the information bottleneck theory, and layers can be frozen based on entropy variability without loss of accuracy, providing a semiotic interpretation of training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The spatial entropy of CNN saliency maps during training exhibits patterns resembling the fitting and compression phases of the information bottleneck theory.
A mutual dependency exists between the information bottleneck theory and the semiotic superization process in deep neural networks.
Layers with low spatial entropy variability can be frozen early during training without significantly impacting network accuracy, enabling a form of layer-wise early stopping.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces computational overhead due to the need to compute spatial entropy during training.
Additional experiments are needed with different DNN architectures and more practical applications to draw stronger conclusions.
A more robust theoretical understanding of the observed phenomena is required.
future_direction: Conduct experiments with different DNN architectures.
Explore more practical applications of spatial entropy variability through time.
Develop a more robust theoretical understanding of the phenomena.
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck principle was recently proposed as a theory meant to explain some of the training dynamics of deep neural architectures. Via information plane analysis, patterns start to emerge in this framework, where two phases can be distinguished: fitting and compression. We take a step further and study the behaviour of the spatial entropy characterizing the layers of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), in relation to the information bottleneck theory. We observe pattern formations which resemble the information bottleneck fitting and compression phases. From the perspective of semiotics, also known as the study of signs and sign-using behavior, the saliency maps of CNN’s layers exhibit aggregations: signs are aggregated into supersigns and this process is called semiotic superization. Superization can be characterized by a decrease of entropy and interpreted as information concentration. We discuss the information bottleneck principle from the perspective of semiotic superization and discover very interesting analogies related to the informational adaptation of the model. In a practical application, we introduce a modification of the CNN training process: we progressively freeze the layers with small entropy variation of their saliency map representation. Such layers can be stopped earlier from training without a significant impact on the performance (the accuracy) of the network, connecting the entropy evolution through time with the training dynamics of a network.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Feature learning is decoupled from generalization in high capacity neural networks
papers.research_question: Do current theories of feature learning measure the quality of learned features (which impacts generalization) or just the strength of representation changes?
papers.core_contribution: Current feature learning theories measure the strength of representation changes (FL strength) but not the quality of features, and these are decoupled. The paper introduces the FL gap to measure feature quality and shows that FL strength does not predict generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current theories of feature learning do not predict generalization because they measure strength rather than quality, indicating the need for a more comprehensive FL theory.
papers.key_findings:
The feature learning gap (∆NT) quantifies the performance improvement of neural networks over kernel methods.
Current FL definitions (NTK-based, CK-based, superposition-based) measure FL strength, not feature quality.
FL strength metrics (e.g., SNT, SCK) fail to distinguish between networks trained on true vs. shuffled labels, indicating decoupling from generalization.
The NTK-based FL strength can be manipulated by output scaling without affecting generalization.
CK-based cumulative utility does not differentiate between shuffled and non-shuffled data.
future_direction: Developing a more comprehensive feature learning theory that links feature learning to generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks outperform kernel methods, sometimes by orders of magnitude, e.g. on staircase functions. This advantage stems from the ability of neural networks to learn features, adapting their hidden representations to better capture the data. We introduce a concept we call feature quality to measure this performance improvement. We examine existing theories of feature learning and demonstrate empirically that they primarily assess the strength of feature learning, rather than the quality of the learned features themselves. Consequently, current theories of feature learning do not provide a sufficient foundation for developing theories of neural network generalization.

papers.title: Learning in PINNs: Phase transition, total diffusion, and generalization
papers.research_question: How do gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and phase transitions affect the training dynamics and generalization of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and can we accelerate convergence by promoting gradient homogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a third training phase called 'total diffusion' characterized by gradient homogeneity and rapid convergence in PINNs, and proposes a residual-based re-weighting scheme (RBA) to accelerate this phase and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: Recognizing phase transitions, particularly the total diffusion phase, can refine optimization strategies for improved generalization in PINNs and potentially other neural network applications.
papers.key_findings:
A third training phase, 'total diffusion', is identified where batch gradients become highly homogeneous, leading to the most rapid convergence.
The proposed RBA re-weighting method accelerates the onset of total diffusion and improves generalization performance in PINNs.
Total diffusion is tightly linked to gradient homogeneity and an abrupt increase in gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
Information compression, observed as saturation ('binarization') of neuron activations, coincides with the transition into total diffusion.
Middle layers of the fully-connected network exhibit the highest saturation during the compression process, reminiscent of an encoder-decoder structure.
papers.abstract: We investigate the learning dynamics of fully-connected neural networks through the lens of gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), examining the behavior of first-order optimizers like Adam in non-convex objectives. By interpreting the drift/diffusion phases in the information bottleneck theory, focusing on gradient homogeneity, we identify a third phase termed ``total diffusion", characterized by equilibrium in the learning rates and homogeneous gradients. This phase is marked by an abrupt SNR increase, uniform residuals across the sample space and the most rapid training convergence. We propose a residual-based re-weighting scheme to accelerate this diffusion in quadratic loss functions, enhancing generalization. We also explore the information compression phenomenon, pinpointing a significant saturation-induced compression of activations at the total diffusion phase, with deeper layers experiencing negligible information loss. Supported by experimental data on physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which underscore the importance of gradient homogeneity due to their PDE-based sample inter-dependence, our findings suggest that recognizing phase transitions could refine ML optimization strategies for improved generalization.

papers.title: Do Wide and Deep Networks Learn the Same Things? Uncovering How Neural Network Representations Vary with Width and Depth
papers.research_question: How do depth and width affect the learned representations of neural networks? Do wide and deep networks learn the same things?
papers.core_contribution: Wide and deep networks develop a block structure in their representations when overparameterized, which arises from preserving and propagating the first principal component. Representations outside the block structure are similar across architectures, but the block structure is unique to each model.
papers.conclusion: Width and depth have distinct effects on neural network representations and predictions, with the block structure being a characteristic of overparameterized models.
papers.key_findings:
Wide and deep networks exhibit a block structure in their hidden representations when overparameterized relative to the dataset.
The block structure arises from the preservation and propagation of the first principal component of the layer representations.
Representations outside the block structure are similar across different architectures and initializations, but the block structure is unique to each model.
Linear probe accuracy plateaus within the block structure, and some layers in the block can be pruned with minimal performance loss.
Wide and deep models make systematically different errors at the example and class levels, even when overall accuracy is similar.
papers.limitation: There remain open questions on how the block structure arises through training and how to use these insights for model design.
future_direction: Understanding how the block structure arises through training
Using insights on depth and width to inform optimal task-specific model design
papers.abstract: A key factor in the success of deep neural networks is the ability to scale models to improve performance by varying the architecture depth and width. This simple property of neural network design has resulted in highly effective architectures for a variety of tasks. Nevertheless, there is limited understanding of effects of depth and width on the learned representations. In this paper, we study this fundamental question. We begin by investigating how varying depth and width affects model hidden representations, finding a characteristic block structure in the hidden representations of larger capacity (wider or deeper) models. We demonstrate that this block structure arises when model capacity is large relative to the size of the training set, and is indicative of the underlying layers preserving and propagating the dominant principal component of their representations. This discovery has important ramifications for features learned by different models, namely, representations outside the block structure are often similar across architectures with varying widths and depths, but the block structure is unique to each model. We analyze the output predictions of different model architectures, finding that even when the overall accuracy is similar, wide and deep models exhibit distinctive error patterns and variations across classes.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Learning Representations in Reinforcement Learning:An Information Bottleneck Approach
papers.research_question: How can the information bottleneck framework be used to learn efficient representations in reinforcement learning to improve sample efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an information bottleneck framework for representation learning in reinforcement learning that improves sample efficiency by accelerating the information extraction-compression process.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes an optimization problem for learning representations in RL based on the information bottleneck framework, derives the optimal target distribution, constructs a lower bound optimized with Stein variational gradient descent, and verifies that the information extraction-compression process exists in deep RL and is accelerated by the framework.
papers.key_findings:
The information extraction-compression process exists in deep reinforcement learning, as observed using mutual information neural estimation (MINE).
The proposed information bottleneck framework accelerates the information extraction-compression process.
Combining actor-critic algorithms (A2C and PPO) with the information bottleneck framework improves sample efficiency compared to vanilla versions.
The framework can be optimized using Stein variational gradient descent via a variational lower bound.
A theoretical algorithm is derived to optimize the framework without constructing a lower bound, using MINE.
papers.limitation: Excessive information dropping by the framework may harm performance in some environments, as observed in SpaceInvaders and MsPacman.
future_direction: Incorporate the information bottleneck method into other off-policy and model-based algorithms.
Experimentally study the derived algorithm based on MINE that directly optimizes the framework without a lower bound.
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck principle is an elegant and useful approach to representation learning. In this paper, we investigate the problem of representation learning in the context of reinforcement learning using the information bottleneck framework, aiming at improving the sample efficiency of the learning algorithms. %by accelerating the process of discarding irrelevant information when the %input states are extremely high-dimensional. We analytically derive the optimal conditional distribution of the representation, and provide a variational lower bound. Then, we maximize this lower bound with the Stein variational (SV) gradient method. We incorporate this framework in the advantageous actor critic algorithm (A2C) and the proximal policy optimization algorithm (PPO). Our experimental results show that our framework can improve the sample efficiency of vanilla A2C and PPO significantly. Finally, we study the information bottleneck (IB) perspective in deep RL with the algorithm called mutual information neural estimation(MINE) . We experimentally verify that the information extraction-compression process also exists in deep RL and our framework is capable of accelerating this process. We also analyze the relationship between MINE and our method, through this relationship, we theoretically derive an algorithm to optimize our IB framework without constructing the lower bound.

papers.title: Binary autoencoder with random binary weights
papers.research_question: How does a binary autoencoder with random binary weights preserve information, and why does sparse activation emerge in the hidden layer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse activation in a binary autoencoder with random binary weights emerges to maximize mutual information between layers, and reveals a memory-computation trade-off between sparse and dense representations.
papers.conclusion: The model provides insights into the memory-computation trade-off in neural representations and is analogous to the fruit fly olfactory system, offering theoretical understanding for more complex networks.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse activation in the hidden layer minimizes reconstruction error and maximizes mutual information between input and output layers.
With a large enough hidden layer, zero reconstruction error is achievable for any input by adjusting thresholds.
Mutual information between input and hidden layer is maximized for dense hidden layer activation, while between input and output layer it is maximized for sparse hidden layer activation.
Similarity preservation (mAP) is best at 50% hidden layer sparsity, not at the sparsity that minimizes error.
The binary matching pursuit (BMP) model gives better reconstruction and sparser activations than threshold and kWTA models.
papers.limitation: The model assumes uniform input distribution and binary activations, which may not reflect real biological systems.
future_direction: Investigate non-uniform input distributions and learning algorithms for binary weights.
Extend the model to spatiotemporal patterns and spiking neural networks.
Explore the connection between mutual information and neural activation function complexity.
papers.abstract: Here is presented an analysis of an autoencoder with binary activations $\{0, 1\}$ and binary $\{0, 1\}$ random weights. Such set up puts this model at the intersection of different fields: neuroscience, information theory, sparse coding, and machine learning. It is shown that the sparse activation of the hidden layer arises naturally in order to preserve information between layers. Furthermore, with a large enough hidden layer, it is possible to get zero reconstruction error for any input just by varying the thresholds of neurons. The model preserves the similarity of inputs at the hidden layer that is maximal for the dense hidden layer activation. By analyzing the mutual information between layers it is shown that the difference between sparse and dense representations is related to a memory-computation trade-off. The model is similar to an olfactory perception system of a fruit fly, and the presented theoretical results give useful insights toward understanding more complex neural networks.

papers.title: Spatial Information Bottleneck for Interpretable Visual Recognition
papers.research_question: Can we explicitly constrain the spatial information structure of neural networks to achieve sharper disentanglement and improve interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Spatial Information Bottleneck (S-IB), a training framework that spatially disentangles information flow by optimizing the spatial structure of Vector-Jacobian Products, leading to improved interpretability and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: S-IB achieves explicit spatial disentanglement during training without requiring annotations, leading to superior interpretability, competitive accuracy, and improved robustness to spurious correlations.
papers.key_findings:
S-IB improves classification accuracy across all 20 dataset-architecture combinations, with up to 3.2% accuracy gains.
S-IB improves the quality of post-hoc explanations across six different methods without method-specific tuning.
S-IB increases foreground mutual information and decreases background mutual information, leading to better spatial disentanglement.
The improvements are more pronounced for CAM-based methods (GradCAM, GradCAM++, ScoreCAM) than for gradient-based methods (Saliency, Guided Backprop, Integrated Gradients).
S-IB suppresses spurious background correlations, as shown in the example of bird reflection.
papers.limitation: The current VJP-based implementation requires second-order gradients during backpropagation, introducing computational overhead.
future_direction: Developing efficient approximations to reduce the computational overhead of second-order gradients.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks typically learn spatially entangled representations that conflate discriminative foreground features with spurious background correlations, thereby undermining model interpretability and robustness. We propose a novel understanding framework for gradient-based attribution from an information-theoretic perspective. We prove that, under mild conditions, the Vector-Jacobian Products (VJP) computed during backpropagation form minimal sufficient statistics of input features with respect to class labels. Motivated by this finding, we propose an encoding-decoding perspective : forward propagation encodes inputs into class space, while VJP in backpropagation decodes this encoding back to feature space. Therefore, we propose Spatial Information Bottleneck (S-IB) to spatially disentangle information flow. By maximizing mutual information between foreground VJP and inputs while minimizing mutual information in background regions, S-IB encourages networks to encode information only in class-relevant spatial regions. Since post-hoc explanation methods fundamentally derive from VJP computations, directly optimizing VJP's spatial structure during training improves visualization quality across diverse explanation paradigms. Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate universal improvements across six explanation methods, achieving better foreground concentration and background suppression without method-specific tuning, alongside consistent classification accuracy gains.

papers.title: An Interpretable Neuron Embedding for Static Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide a sample- and class-independent explanation of neurons in a model, and can static knowledge from neuron semantics be used for knowledge distillation without sample-by-sample guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to embed neurons into semantic vectors for interpretability, enabling static knowledge distillation that performs comparably to existing methods without sample-by-sample teacher guidance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes neuron embedding for interpretability and static knowledge distillation, demonstrating effective knowledge transfer without instance-specific guidance.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic vectors accurately represent neuron semantics, as shown by similar activation maps for neurons with similar vectors.
The embedding method spontaneously converges to manually annotated semantic vectors without supervision.
Static knowledge distillation achieves performance comparable to or better than existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.
The method allows for analysis of neuron similar and additive relations.
Without sample-by-sample guidance, SKD is efficient and scalable.
papers.abstract: Although deep neural networks have shown well-performance in various tasks, the poor interpretability of the models is always criticized. In the paper, we propose a new interpretable neural network method, by embedding neurons into the semantic space to extract their intrinsic global semantics. In contrast to previous methods that probe latent knowledge inside the model, the proposed semantic vector externalizes the latent knowledge to static knowledge, which is easy to exploit. Specifically, we assume that neurons with similar activation are of similar semantic information. Afterwards, semantic vectors are optimized by continuously aligning activation similarity and semantic vector similarity during the training of the neural network. The visualization of semantic vectors allows for a qualitative explanation of the neural network. Moreover, we assess the static knowledge quantitatively by knowledge distillation tasks. Empirical experiments of visualization show that semantic vectors describe neuron activation semantics well. Without the sample-by-sample guidance from the teacher model, static knowledge distillation exhibit comparable or even superior performance with existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.

papers.title: Modeling the Influence of Data Structure on Learning in Neural Networks: The Hidden Manifold Model
papers.research_question: How does the structure of data (specifically, data lying on a lower-dimensional manifold) affect the learning dynamics and generalization performance of two-layer neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hidden Manifold Model (HMM), a generative model for structured data, and proves a Gaussian Equivalence Property (GEP) that enables analytical derivation of learning dynamics for two-layer neural networks trained with online stochastic gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The Hidden Manifold Model provides a tractable framework for studying how data structure influences learning in neural networks, and the analytical results offer insights into the dynamics of specialization and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The Gaussian Equivalence Property holds for the HMM, allowing the learning dynamics to be described by a set of integro-differential equations.
Neural networks learn functions of increasing complexity during training, with a specialization transition where hidden units gradually align with teacher nodes.
Generalization performance deteriorates as the manifold dimension increases and improves with network width, but saturates beyond a certain width.
The learning rate has a minor influence on asymptotic error, but affects the time to reach specialization.
The HMM captures key properties of real data sets (MNIST, CIFAR10) in terms of learning dynamics and memorization patterns.
papers.abstract: Understanding the reasons for the success of deep neural networks trained using stochastic gradientbased methods is a key open problem for the nascent theory of deep learning. The types of data where these networks are most successful, such as images or sequences of speech, are characterized by intricate correlations. Yet, most theoretical work on neural networks does not explicitly model training data or assumes that elements of each data sample are drawn independently from some factorized probability distribution. These approaches are, thus, by construction blind to the correlation structure of real-world datasets and their impact on learning in neural networks. Here, we introduce a generative model for structured datasets that we call the hidden manifold model. The idea is to construct high-dimensional inputs that lie on a lower-dimensional manifold, with labels that depend only on their position within this manifold, akin to a single-layer decoder or generator in a generative adversarial network. We demonstrate that learning of the hidden manifold model is amenable to an analytical treatment by proving a "Gaussian equivalence property" (GEP), and we use the GEP to show how the dynamics of two-layer neural networks trained using one-pass stochastic gradient descent is captured by a set of integro-differential equations that track the performance of the network at all times. This approach permits us to analyze in detail how a neural network learns functions of increasing complexity during training, how its performance depends on its size, and how it is impacted by parameters such as the learning rate or the dimension of the hidden manifold.

papers.title: The Analysis of Deep Neural Networks by Information Theory: From Explainability to Generalization
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews information-theoretic approaches for analyzing deep neural networks, focusing on explainability and generalization, and highlights the authors' contributions including matrix-based entropy functionals and applications to graph neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Information theory offers fresh insights and tools to address challenges in explainability and generalization for deep neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Matrix-based entropy functionals enable efficient estimation of information-theoretic quantities from samples without density estimation or neural network training.
The Information Bottleneck principle provides mathematically well-founded methods to understand the inner mechanisms of DNNs during training.
Information theory helps determine tighter lower bounds for generalization error in DNNs.
Information-theoretic methods can design robust loss functions under distributional shift and quantify domain relatedness.
The principles can be transferred to design novel graph neural networks for brain network analysis, improving explainability and generalization.
papers.abstract: Despite their great success in many artificial intelligence tasks, deep neural networks (DNNs) still suffer from a few limitations, such as poor generalization behavior for out-of-distribution (OOD) data and the "black-box" nature. Information theory offers fresh insights to solve these challenges. In this short paper, we briefly review the recent developments in this area, and highlight our contributions.

papers.title: Exponential Capacity in an Autoencoder Neural Network with a Hidden Layer
papers.research_question: What is the maximal storage capacity of an autoencoder neural network with a hidden layer? The paper shows that the capacity grows exponentially with the expansion ratio.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the storage capacity of an autoencoder with an expansive hidden layer grows exponentially with the expansion ratio, due to many small pairwise correlations between hidden units and output.
papers.conclusion: Using Gardner's replica method and a mean-field approximation, the paper derives the exponential capacity of an expansive autoencoder, which provides a lower bound for the full model and deepens understanding of the role of expansive hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
The capacity of the mean-field approximation model grows exponentially with the expansion ratio Λ.
The full autoencoder model has a higher capacity than the mean-field approximation, indicating the mean-field approximation is a lower bound.
The degree of symmetry between encoding and decoding weights monotonically increases with the expansion ratio.
Exponential capacity persists even when sparseness is introduced in the hidden layer representation.
Exponential capacity also persists with non-zero robustness margins, though the growth rate decreases.
papers.limitation:
The mean-field approximation yields a lower capacity than the full model because it ignores higher-order correlations.
Robustness to input noise (e.g., bit flips) may reduce capacity and requires further investigation.
future_direction: Investigating how optimizing encoding weights, diluted connectivity, or adding more hidden layers affects the trade-off between capacity and robustness to input noise.
Extending the framework to deep autoencoders and feedforward networks used for classification.
papers.abstract: A fundamental aspect of limitations in learning any computation in neural architectures is characterizing their optimal capacities. An important, widely-used neural architecture is known as autoencoders where the network reconstructs the input at the output layer via a representation at a hidden layer. Even though capacities of several neural architectures have been addressed using statistical physics methods, the capacity of autoencoder neural networks is not well-explored. Here, we analytically show that an autoencoder network of binary neurons with a hidden layer can achieve a capacity that grows exponentially with network size. The network has fixed random weights encoding a set of dense input patterns into a dense, expanded (or \emph{overcomplete}) hidden layer representation. A set of learnable weights decodes the input patters at the output layer. We perform a mean-field approximation of the model to reduce the model to a perceptron problem with an input-output dependency. Carrying out Gardner's \emph{replica} calculation, we show that as the expansion ratio, defined as the number of hidden units over the number of input units, increases, the autoencoding capacity grows exponentially even when the sparseness or the coding level of the hidden layer representation is changed. The replica-symmetric solution is locally stable and is in good agreement with simulation results obtained using a local learning rule. In addition, the degree of symmetry between the encoding and decoding weights monotonically increases with the expansion ratio.

papers.title: Readout Representation: Redefining Neural Codes by Input Recovery
papers.research_question: How does a system that abstracts away details still preserve the fine-grained information needed for downstream functions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the readout representation framework that defines representation by functional recoverability rather than causal origin, and proposes representation size as a metric to quantify the robustness of representations.
papers.conclusion: The readout representation framework offers a new lens for analyzing how both biological and artificial neural systems learn abstract features while maintaining robust, information-rich representations of the world.
papers.key_findings:
Inputs can be accurately reconstructed from heavily perturbed features in lower to middle layers of various vision and language models.
Representation size is larger for correctly classified images than misclassified ones, and zero for noise images.
Representation size correlates with feature dimensionality in vision models, but this trend weakens in higher layers.
The readout representation framework naturally accounts for phenomena like misrepresentation, illusion, and dreaming.
A single input corresponds to a broad, continuous region in feature space from which it can be recovered, indicating inherent redundancy.
papers.abstract: Sensory representation is typically understood through a hierarchical-causal framework where progressively abstract features are extracted sequentially. However, this causal view fails to explain misrepresentation, a phenomenon better handled by an informational view based on decodable content. This creates a tension: how does a system that abstracts away details still preserve the fine-grained information needed for downstream functions? We propose readout representation to resolve this, defining representation by the information recoverable from features rather than their causal origin. Empirically, we show that inputs can be accurately reconstructed even from heavily perturbed mid-level features, demonstrating that a single input corresponds to a broad, redundant region of feature space, challenging the causal mapping perspective. To quantify this property, we introduce representation size, a metric linked to model robustness and representational redundancy. Our framework offers a new lens for analyzing how both biological and artificial neural systems learn complex features while maintaining robust, information-rich representations of the world.

papers.title: Beyond Single Concept Vector: Modeling Concept Subspace in LLMs with Gaussian Distribution
papers.research_question: Instead of using a single vector to describe each underlying concept captured by LLMs, can we use a distribution (specifically a Gaussian distribution) to more robustly describe that learned concept?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Gaussian Concept Subspace (GCS), a method to represent concepts in LLMs as a Gaussian distribution of vectors, which is more robust than single vectors and effective for concept representation and emotion steering.
papers.conclusion: GCS offers a concise yet powerful method for concept subspace estimation, showing promise in both theoretical explanations and practical applications.
papers.key_findings:
GCS-sampled concept vectors are faithful and plausible, showing high similarity to observed vectors and comparable or better accuracy.
GCS reveals hierarchical concept structures that align with human understanding.
GCS vectors are effective in inference-time intervention for emotion steering, balancing steering performance and fluency.
Sampled vectors within 1σ and 2σ achieve better prediction accuracy than observed vectors.
The method is robust across different model architectures and sizes (Llama-2-7B, Gemma-7B, Llama-2-13B).
papers.limitation: Evaluating GCS at the distribution level is challenging due to the infinite potential of sampled vectors and the variability in relevance with distance from the mean.
papers.abstract: Probing learned concepts in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for understanding how semantic knowledge is encoded internally. Training linear classifiers on probing tasks is a principle approach to denote the vector of a certain concept in the representation space. However, the single vector identified for a concept varies with both data and training, making it less robust and weakening its effectiveness in real-world applications. To address this challenge, we propose an approach to approximate the subspace representing a specific concept. Built on linear probing classifiers, we extend the concept vectors into Gaussian Concept Subspace (GCS). We demonstrate GCS's effectiveness through measuring its faithfulness and plausibility across multiple LLMs with different sizes and architectures. Additionally, we use representation intervention tasks to showcase its efficacy in real-world applications such as emotion steering. Experimental results indicate that GCS concept vectors have the potential to balance steering performance and maintaining the fluency in natural language generation tasks.

papers.title: An Information Theoretic Interpretation to Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the mathematical meaning of informative features in deep neural networks (DNNs)? How can we interpret the internal computations and weight updates in DNNs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides an information-theoretic interpretation of DNNs, showing that feature extraction in DNNs coincides with the solution of a universal feature selection problem, and that weight updates can be interpreted as projecting features between feature spaces via SVD.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic framework provides an interpretation to the internal computations of DNNs, connecting feature selection to an optimization problem with operational meaning for inference tasks.
papers.key_findings:
In the local analysis regime, the optimal features selected by DNNs from log-loss optimization coincide with the solutions of universal feature selection.
DNN weight updates can be interpreted as projecting features between the feature spaces of data and label to extract the most correlated aspects.
The iterative projections in backpropagation can be viewed as computing the SVD of a linear projection between feature spaces.
The proposed H-score measures the quality of features extracted by an intermediate layer and has a clear upper bound.
Experimental validation on synthetic data and ImageNet shows consistency between theory and practice.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is valid only in the local regime (small ϵ)
Limited expressive power of the network may prevent achieving the optimal feature function
papers.abstract: It is commonly believed that the hidden layers of deep neural networks (DNNs) attempt to extract informative features for learning tasks. In this paper, we formalize this intuition by showing that the features extracted by DNN coincide with the result of an optimization problem, which we call the `universal feature selection' problem, in a local analysis regime. We interpret the weights training in DNN as the projection of feature functions between feature spaces, specified by the network structure. Our formulation has direct operational meaning in terms of the performance for inference tasks, and gives interpretations to the internal computation results of DNNs. Results of numerical experiments are provided to support the analysis.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: Why do LLaVA Vision-Language Models Reply to Images in English?
papers.research_question: Why do LLaVA-style vision-language models tend to reply in English when queried in other languages with an image?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes Image-induced Fidelity Loss (IFL) in LLaVA-style vision-language models, showing that the issue stems from the language model and that using a bilingual language backbone reduces the error.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that IFL is a significant issue in multilingual VLMs, primarily due to the language model, and suggests that improving the multilinguality of LLMs is key to building robust multilingual VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Adding an image to a query in a non-English language increases the likelihood of an English response (Image-induced Fidelity Loss).
Switching the language backbone from a monolingual to a bilingual model reduces IFL.
Visual inputs are not mapped to a similar space as text inputs in the model's representations.
Intervening on intermediary attention layers in the language model can reduce IFL.
Changing the vision encoder or training data language can worsen IFL without affecting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The assumption that the expert annotations for language identification are correct.
The analysis of embeddings involves some speculation and does not definitively prove that inputs are mapped to distinct semantic spaces.
Lack of focus on second- and third-order interactions, especially differences in IFL between languages.
Ethical risks of externalizing the contextualization and nuance necessary for truly inclusive goals, especially when the authors do not speak all languages studied.
future_direction: Considering language fidelity during training through multilingual data and language-controlling instructions.
Designing better model architectures that integrate multimodal representations at a suitable semantic level to prevent language bias.
Improving the mechanistic intervention, such as automatic attribute selection or better construction of the attribute.
papers.abstract: Musashi Hinck, Carolin Holtermann, Matthew Lyle Olson, Florian Schneider, Sungduk Yu, Anahita Bhiwandiwalla, Anne Lauscher, Shao-Yen Tseng, Vasudev Lal. Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024. 2024.

papers.title: Understanding Neural Networks and Individual Neuron Importance via Information-Ordered Cumulative Ablation
papers.research_question: How do information-theoretic quantities (entropy, mutual information, and KL selectivity) relate to the classification performance and importance of individual neurons in trained neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that information-theoretic quantities (mutual information and KL selectivity) are positively correlated with neuron importance for classification when analyzed layer-wise, but not when compared across layers, and introduces information-ordered cumulative ablation as a method to study redundancy and synergy in neural network layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that it is ill-advised to compare information-theoretic quantities across layers due to their differing distributions, and that layer-wise analysis reveals a positive correlation between these quantities and neuron importance for classification, particularly in ReLU networks.
papers.key_findings:
Class selectivity is not a good indicator for classification performance when comparing neurons across different layers.
When analyzing neurons within a single layer, mutual information and class selectivity are positively correlated with classification performance, at least for networks with ReLU activation functions.
Information-ordered cumulative ablation can be used to formulate hypotheses about the redundancy and synergy of neurons within a layer.
The distribution of information-theoretic quantities (entropy, mutual information, KL selectivity) changes across layers, with deeper layers generally having higher values.
The correlation between these information-theoretic quantities and classification performance depends on the activation function and the regularization method used during training.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are restricted to fully-connected neural networks; results for convolutional, recurrent, or residual networks are not provided.
Results for networks with sigmoid activation functions or trained with batch normalization are inconclusive, showing at most weak correlation.
The quantization scheme used to estimate information-theoretic quantities is coarse, which may affect results.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other neural network classes such as convolutional, recurrent, or residual networks.
Investigate the use of finer quantization schemes to better estimate information-theoretic quantities.
Apply partial information decomposition (PID) to account for redundancy and synergy in neural network layers.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate the use of three information-theoretic quantities-entropy, mutual information with the class variable, and a class selectivity measure based on Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence-to understand and study the behavior of already trained fully connected feedforward neural networks (NNs). We analyze the connection between these information-theoretic quantities and classification performance on the test set by cumulatively ablating neurons in networks trained on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10. Our results parallel those recently published by Morcos et al., indicating that class selectivity is not a good indicator for classification performance.
