However, looking at individual layers separately, both mutual information and class selectivity are positively correlated with classification performance, at least for networks with ReLU activation functions. We provide explanations for this phenomenon and conclude that it is ill-advised to compare the proposed information-theoretic quantities across layers. Furthermore, we show that cumulative ablation of neurons with ascending or descending information-theoretic quantities can be used to formulate hypotheses regarding the joint behavior of multiple neurons, such as redundancy and synergy, with comparably low computational cost. We also draw connections to the information bottleneck theory for NNs.

papers.title: Unpacking Information Bottlenecks: Unifying Information-Theoretic Objectives in Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How can we develop tractable surrogate objectives for the Information Bottleneck principle that scale to modern deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops tractable surrogate objectives for the Information Bottleneck principle, enabling its application to modern deep neural networks without complex estimators.
papers.conclusion: The proposed surrogate objectives enable the application of Information Bottleneck principles to modern deep neural networks, yielding improved robustness and interpretable training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Surrogate objectives based on Decoder Cross-Entropy and simple regularizers (like L2 norm of latent) can approximate IB objectives.
Adding zero-entropy noise to latent representations is necessary to avoid pathological optimization with differential entropies.
Models trained with these surrogate objectives show improved adversarial robustness compared to standard training.
The training trajectories in the information plane show the expected trade-off between compression and performance.
The Decoder Cross-Entropy is a better training objective than the Prediction Cross-Entropy for stochastic models.
papers.abstract: The Information Bottleneck principle offers both a mechanism to explain how deep neural networks train and generalize, as well as a regularized objective with which to train models. However, multiple competing objectives are proposed in the literature, and the information-theoretic quantities used in these objectives are difficult to compute for large deep neural networks, which in turn limits their use as a training objective. In this work, we review these quantities and compare and unify previously proposed objectives, which allows us to develop surrogate objectives more friendly to optimization without relying on cumbersome tools such as density estimation. We find that these surrogate objectives allow us to apply the information bottleneck to modern neural network architectures. We demonstrate our insights on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and Imagenette with modern DNN architectures (ResNets).

papers.title: A Generalized Information Bottleneck Theory of Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How can the Information Bottleneck principle be reformulated to address its theoretical ambiguities and estimation challenges, and to capture synergistic interactions between features for better generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Generalized Information Bottleneck (GIB) framework, which reformulates the Information Bottleneck principle through the lens of synergy, providing more consistent compression phases and interpretable learning dynamics across diverse neural network architectures.
papers.conclusion: The GIB framework addresses longstanding limitations of the original IB and provides a more complete picture of how deep networks process information through synergistic feature interactions.
papers.key_findings:
GIB exhibits compression phases across a wide range of architectures (including ReLU) where standard IB fails.
Synergistic functions lead to better generalization, as shown theoretically and empirically.
GIB's complexity term reflects adversarial vulnerability better than standard IB, correctly tracking degradation under attack.
GIB provides interpretable information dynamics in both CNNs and Transformers during training.
Under perfect estimation, GIB is upper bounded by the original IB, ensuring theoretical compatibility.
papers.limitation:
Mutual information estimation methods (e.g., binning) can introduce substantial estimation error.
GIB requires more computations than standard IB due to feature-wise synergy decomposition.
papers.abstract: The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle offers a compelling theoretical framework to understand how neural networks (NNs) learn. However, its practical utility has been constrained by unresolved theoretical ambiguities and significant challenges in accurate estimation. In this paper, we present a \textit{Generalized Information Bottleneck (GIB)} framework that reformulates the original IB principle through the lens of synergy, i.e., the information obtainable only through joint processing of features. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrating that synergistic functions achieve superior generalization compared to their non-synergistic counterparts. Building on these foundations we re-formulate the IB using a computable definition of synergy based on the average interaction information (II) of each feature with those remaining. We demonstrate that the original IB objective is upper bounded by our GIB in the case of perfect estimation, ensuring compatibility with existing IB theory while addressing its limitations. Our experimental results demonstrate that GIB consistently exhibits compression phases across a wide range of architectures (including those with \textit{ReLU} activations where the standard IB fails), while yielding interpretable dynamics in both CNNs and Transformers and aligning more closely with our understanding of adversarial robustness.

papers.title: Letters of the Alphabet: Discovering Natural Feature Sets
papers.research_question: How do hidden layers in a simple neural network represent input features, and how can natural feature sets be derived from the data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how hidden node activations in a neural network can be visualized to understand feature representation and how natural feature sets can be discovered by grouping similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide a step-by-step blueprint for how neural networks derive natural feature sets from data, offering insights into feature representation in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden nodes in the network activate to specific features like vertical and horizontal bars in letter representations.
Nodes 2 and 5 are activated strongly by most letters, indicating potential overfitting or redundancy.
Natural feature sets group similarly shaped letters, such as A and H, or B, R, and P.
Adding 10% noise did not improve generalization in the natural feature sets experiment.
Heatmap visualizations effectively show which input patterns contribute to hidden node activations.
papers.limitation:
Adding 10% noise did not help the hidden nodes generalize better as expected.
Deciphering and visualizing hidden node activations took a lot of time and explanation.
future_direction: Spend more time formatting visualizations to efficiently display hidden node activations for natural feature sets.
Use algorithms to automatically determine the ideal number of hidden nodes to speed up development.
papers.abstract: Deep learning networks find intricate features in large datasets using the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm repeatedly adjusts the network connections.' weights and examining the "hidden" nodes behavior between the input and output layer provides better insight into how neural networks create feature representations. Experiments built on each other show that activity differences computed within a layer can guide learning. A simple neural network is used, which includes a data set comprised of the alphabet letters, where each letter forms 81 input nodes comprised of 0 and 1s and a single hidden layer and an output layer. The first experiment explains how the hidden layers in this simple neural network represent the input data's features. The second experiment attempts to reverse-engineer the neural network to find the alphabet's natural feature sets. As the network interprets features, we can understand how it derives the natural feature sets for a given data. This understanding is essential to delve deeper into deep generative models, such as Boltzmann machines. Deep generative models are a class of unsupervised deep learning algorithms. The primary function of deep generative models is to find the natural feature sets for a given data set.

papers.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do abstract representations emerge in neural networks? Specifically, the paper investigates whether abstract representations are guaranteed to appear in feedforward networks trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical theory proving that abstract representations are guaranteed to emerge in the hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables, and develops a mean-field optimization framework to analyze such representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained on tasks with latent variables, providing a mathematical explanation for similar observations in neuroscience and machine learning, and offers a general framework for understanding representation geometry in task-optimized networks.
papers.key_findings:
For whitened and target-aligned inputs, ReLU networks develop abstract representations with parallelism score (PS) equal to 1 at global minima.
The optimal representation kernel takes the form K = a*11^T + b*K_Y, where K_Y is the output kernel.
The emergence of abstract representations is robust to the choice of activation function, holding for two broad classes of nonlinearities: threshold functions and odd functions.
The theory extends to multi-element classes (n ≥ 2) and deep feedforward architectures.
The framework provides a mean-field description where the optimal preactivation distribution satisfies a self-consistent condition.
papers.limitation:
The theory is limited to feedforward networks trained on tasks with binary latent variables and assumes the network reaches a global minimum.
The analysis assumes specific input geometries (whitened or target-aligned inputs) and may not cover all possible input structures.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures such as ResNet and transformer models.
Analyze learning dynamics in networks trained with biological learning rules.
Investigate the Platonic representation hypothesis using the developed mathematical toolkit.
papers.abstract: Recent experiments reveal that task-relevant variables are often encoded in approximately orthogonal subspaces of the neural activity space. These disentangled low-dimensional representations are observed in multiple brain areas and across different species, and are typically the result of a process of abstraction that supports simple forms of out-of-distribution generalization. The mechanisms by which such geometries emerge remain poorly understood, and the mechanisms that have been investigated are typically unsupervised (e.g., based on variational auto-encoders). Here, we show mathematically that abstract representations of latent variables are guaranteed to appear in the last hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when they are trained on tasks that depend directly on these latent variables. These abstract representations reflect the structure of the desired outputs or the semantics of the input stimuli. To investigate the neural representations that emerge in these networks, we develop an analytical framework that maps the optimization over the network weights into a mean-field problem over the distribution of neural preactivations. Applying this framework to a finite-width ReLU network, we find that its hidden layer exhibits an abstract representation at all global minima of the task objective. We further extend these analyses to two broad families of activation functions and deep feedforward architectures, demonstrating that abstract representations naturally arise in all these scenarios. Together, these results provide an explanation for the widely observed abstract representations in both the brain and artificial neural networks, as well as a mathematically tractable toolkit for understanding the emergence of different kinds of representations in task-optimized, feature-learning network models.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Internal and collective interpretation for improving human interpretability of multi-layered neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the inference mechanism of neural networks internally (without external methods) and collectively (considering all internal representations from different conditions and patterns)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new interpretation method that combines internal and collective interpretation, using information augmentation to compensate for information loss during compression, and shows that the compressed weights resemble linear correlation coefficients.
papers.conclusion: The proposed internal and collective interpretation method with information augmentation can improve generalization performance and produce interpretable weights that reflect linear correlations, offering a way to understand neural networks without external explanation methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method with information augmentation and compression improves generalization performance compared to conventional methods like logistic regression and ensemble methods.
The compressed or collective weights from multi-layered networks tend to produce weights similar to linear correlation coefficients between inputs and targets.
The information augmentation component helps disentangle complex features into simpler ones, facilitating interpretation.
The method enables internal interpretation of the inference mechanism without relying on external methods like symbolic rules.
Collective interpretation, which considers all internal representations from different initial conditions and patterns, provides a more stable and comprehensive understanding of the model.
papers.limitation: Competitive learning, used for mutual information maximization, has the well-known shortcoming of dead neurons, where some neurons cannot be used in learning, which contradicts the goal of using all neurons equally.
future_direction: Examine to what extent the method can be used to clarify the actual meaning of data sets.

Examine in what points the present method is different from the linear correlations between inputs and targets, and explain why and how the difference can be produced for the further development of neural networks.
papers.abstract: The present paper aims to propose a new type of information-theoretic method to interpret the inference mechanism of neural networks. We interpret the internal inference mechanism for itself without any external methods such as symbolic or fuzzy rules. In addition, we make interpretation processes as stable as possible. This means that we interpret the inference mechanism, considering all internal representations, created by those different conditions and patterns. To make the internal interpretation possible, we try to compress multi-layered neural networks into the simplest ones without hidden layers. Then, the natural information loss in the process of compression is complemented by the introduction of a mutual information augmentation component. The method was applied to two data sets, namely, the glass data set and the pregnancy data set. In both data sets, information augmentation and compression methods could improve generalization performance. In addition, compressed or collective weights from the multi-layered networks tended to produce weights, ironically, similar to the linear correlation coefficients between inputs and targets, while the conventional methods such as the logistic regression analysis failed to do so.

papers.title: VisBERT: Hidden-State Visualizations for Transformers
papers.research_question: How do BERT models transform token representations across layers during Question Answering tasks, and what insights can be gained from visualizing these hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VisBERT, a tool for visualizing hidden states in BERT for QA, enabling insights into semantic transformations and identifying four distinct phases in BERT's inference process.
papers.conclusion: VisBERT provides a novel visualization method for BERT's hidden states, revealing consistent inference phases across QA tasks that resemble traditional NLP pipelines.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's inference involves four phases: topical clustering, connecting entities with mentions and attributes, matching questions with supporting facts, and answer extraction.
VisBERT visualizations reveal how token representations change across layers, similar to a traditional NLP pipeline.
The tool can identify failure states, such as wrong supporting fact selection or degenerate phases, by observing clusters in hidden states.
Visualizations show that model confidence correlates with distinctness of clusters in each layer.
Adversarial examples can be explored to detect biases and shortcomings in QA models using hidden state visualizations.
future_direction: Extending VisBERT to other BERT models, different QA datasets, and other NLP tasks, as well as to other Transformer-based models like GPT-2.
Incorporating other dimensionality reduction methods like t-SNE or UMAP.
Exploring modularity in BERT's phases for fine-tuning different layers on upstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Explainability and interpretability are two important concepts, the absence of which can and should impede the application of well-performing neural networks to real-world problems. At the same time, they are difficult to incorporate into the large, black-box models that achieve state-of-the-art results in a multitude of NLP tasks. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) is one such black-box model. It has become a staple architecture to solve many different NLP tasks and has inspired a number of related Transformer models. Understanding how these models draw conclusions is crucial for both their improvement and application. We contribute to this challenge by presenting VisBERT, a tool for visualizing the contextual token representations within BERT for the task of (multi-hop) Question Answering. Instead of analyzing attention weights, we focus on the hidden states resulting from each encoder block within the BERT model. This way we can observe how the semantic representations are transformed throughout the layers of the model. VisBERT enables users to get insights about the model's internal state and to explore its inference steps or potential shortcomings. The tool allows us to identify distinct phases in BERT's transformations that are similar to a traditional NLP pipeline and offer insights during failed predictions.

papers.title: An Information Theoretic Approach to Reveal the Formation of Shared Representations
papers.research_question: How does network depth and input mixing affect the formation of shared representations (modality-invariant categorical representations) in a bimodal autoencoder?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information theoretic approach to analyze the formation of shared representations in a bimodal autoencoder, demonstrating that deeper networks and a mixed-input framework enhance the development of modality-invariant categorical representations.
papers.conclusion: The information theoretic approach helps understand the formation of shared representations, and deeper networks with mixed-input frameworks facilitate better shared representations in bimodal autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Shared representations (consistent visual and auditory cells) are formed in the autoencoder's hidden layers.
The number of cells forming shared representations increases with the depth of the network's encoding layers.
The mixed-input framework (concatenating modalities from the start) yields more shared representation cells than the two-stage framework (separate feature learning followed by correlation learning).
Classification performance in a shared-representation learning task is better with the mixed-input framework than the two-stage framework.
The information theoretic approach provides a quantitative measure of representation quality in hidden layers.
papers.abstract: Modality-invariant categorical representations, i.e., shared representation, is thought to play a key role in learning to categorize multi-modal information. We have investigated how a bimodal autoencoder can form a shared representation in an unsupervised manner with multi-modal data. We explored whether altering the depth of the network and mixing the multi-modal inputs at the input layer affect the development of the shared representations. Based on the activation of units in the hidden layers, we classified them into four different types: visual cells, auditory cells, inconsistent visual and auditory cells, and consistent visual and auditory cells. Our results show that the number and quality of the last type (i.e., shared representation) significantly differ depending on the depth of the network and are enhanced when the network receives mixed inputs as opposed to separate inputs for each modality, as occurs in typical two-stage frameworks. In the present work, we present a way to utilize information theory to understand the abstract representations formed in the hidden layers of the network. We believe that such an information theoretic approach could potentially provide insights into the development of more efficient and cost-effective ways to train neural networks using qualitative measures of the representations that cannot be captured by analyzing only the final outputs of the networks.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How do different strategies for extracting lexical type-level knowledge from pretrained language models impact performance across languages and tasks? Is lexical knowledge concentrated in few parameters or scattered? How do these representations compare to traditional static word vectors? Do monolingual LMs learn similar representations for translation pairs?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic study of how to extract lexical type-level knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that lexical information is concentrated in lower layers and that extracted representations can outperform traditional static word embeddings in some tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effective extraction depends on configuration choices such as using monolingual LMs, averaging over lower layers, and excluding special tokens.
papers.key_findings:
Monolingual LMs contain more lexical information than multilingual LMs.
Lexical information is concentrated in lower Transformer layers.
Averaging over multiple layers (especially lower ones) yields better representations than single layers.
Excluding special tokens [CLS] and [SEP] improves performance.
Extracted representations can outperform fastText in monolingual tasks but underperform in cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect AOC configurations and sampling representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, tasks, and larger underlying LMs.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods (e.g., layer weighting or attention).
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-of-context versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Transformers with Competitive Ensembles of Independent Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How can we design a Transformer architecture that better captures independent mechanisms by dividing the hidden representation and parameters into multiple mechanisms that interact via attention and competition?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Transformers with Independent Mechanisms (TIM), a new Transformer layer that divides hidden representations and parameters into multiple mechanisms that interact via attention and competition, leading to improved specialization and performance on image, speech, and language tasks.
papers.conclusion: TIM makes the Transformer more dynamic by breaking the hidden representation into multiple mechanisms that specialize and improve performance, suggesting room for improving structural inductive biases in Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
TIM mechanisms specialize in semantically meaningful ways, e.g., in images, one mechanism focuses on foreground and another on background.
TIM improves performance on speech enhancement, achieving state-of-the-art PESQ on the DNS dataset.
TIM improves BERT pre-training (lower perplexity) and fine-tuning (higher accuracy on GLUE tasks).
TIM improves accuracy on the CATER video object tracking task.
The competition mechanism leads to more confident specialization in deeper layers.
future_direction: Combining the Switch Transformer with TIM could be a fruitful area for future research.
papers.abstract: An important development in deep learning from the earliest MLPs has been a move towards architectures with structural inductive biases which enable the model to keep distinct sources of information and routes of processing well-separated. This structure is linked to the notion of independent mechanisms from the causality literature, in which a mechanism is able to retain the same processing as irrelevant aspects of the world are changed. For example, convnets enable separation over positions, while attention-based architectures (especially Transformers) learn which combination of positions to process dynamically. In this work we explore a way in which the Transformer architecture is deficient: it represents each position with a large monolithic hidden representation and a single set of parameters which are applied over the entire hidden representation. This potentially throws unrelated sources of information together, and limits the Transformer's ability to capture independent mechanisms. To address this, we propose Transformers with Independent Mechanisms (TIM), a new Transformer layer which divides the hidden representation and parameters into multiple mechanisms, which only exchange information through attention. Additionally, we propose a competition mechanism which encourages these mechanisms to specialize over time steps, and thus be more independent. We study TIM on a large-scale BERT model, on the Image Transformer, and on speech enhancement and find evidence for semantically meaningful specialization as well as improved performance.

papers.title: The Neural Race Reduction: Dynamics of Abstraction in Gated Networks
papers.research_question: How does network architecture (specifically pathways of information flow) affect learning dynamics, representation learning, and generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Gated Deep Linear Network framework and shows that learning dynamics exhibit a neural race bias towards shared representations, enabling systematic generalization and multi-task transfer.
papers.conclusion: The GDLN framework reveals how architecture controls information flow and learning dynamics, leading to a bias towards shared representations that enables systematic generalization and multi-task learning.
papers.key_findings:
The GDLN framework allows exact reduction of learning dynamics to singular value dynamics.
Learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race, with faster learning for pathways that share more structure.
There is an implicit bias towards shared representations, which facilitates zero-shot generalization to untrained input-output pathways.
The dynamics from small random weights converge to the maximally shared solution, as validated on naturalistic datasets.
The degree of sharing required for generalization depends on the fraction of trained pathways, with around 40% sufficient for strong generalization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not provide a mechanism to select the gating structure; it is assumed to be given.
The theoretical analysis assumes diagonalizable dataset statistics and linear networks with gating, though validation is done with relaxed assumptions.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for inferring the optimal architecture and gating for a given setup.
papers.abstract: Our theoretical understanding of deep learning has not kept pace with its empirical success. While network architecture is known to be critical, we do not yet understand its effect on learned representations and network behavior, or how this architecture should reflect task structure.In this work, we begin to address this gap by introducing the Gated Deep Linear Network framework that schematizes how pathways of information flow impact learning dynamics within an architecture. Crucially, because of the gating, these networks can compute nonlinear functions of their input. We derive an exact reduction and, for certain cases, exact solutions to the dynamics of learning. Our analysis demonstrates that the learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race with an implicit bias towards shared representations, which then govern the model's ability to systematically generalize, multi-task, and transfer. We validate our key insights on naturalistic datasets and with relaxed assumptions. Taken together, our work gives rise to general hypotheses relating neural architecture to learning and provides a mathematical approach towards understanding the design of more complex architectures and the role of modularity and compositionality in solving real-world problems. The code and results are available at https://www.saxelab.org/gated-dln .

papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: A Probabilistic Representation of Deep Learning for Improving The Information Theoretic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we improve the information-theoretic interpretability of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) by proposing a probabilistic representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a probabilistic representation for MLPs, defining a probability space for fully connected layers and showing the entire MLP corresponds to a Gibbs distribution. This foundation leads to new information-theoretic explanations, including that the Information Bottleneck theory does not hold when back-propagation is considered.
papers.conclusion: The proposed probabilistic representation establishes a solid foundation for information-theoretic interpretability of MLPs, resolving existing controversies and providing novel explanations for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Activations in MLPs are not i.i.d., invalidating non-parametric mutual information estimators for all hidden layers.
A probability space (ΩF, 𝓕, PF) can be defined for a fully connected layer, where the Gibbs measure PF depends on the activation function.
The entire architecture of an MLP can be expressed as a Gibbs distribution.
Back-propagation training optimizes the sample spaces of all layers to learn an optimal Gibbs distribution modeling the statistical connection between input and label.
The Information Bottleneck theory cannot correctly explain the information flow in MLPs when back-propagation is considered, and generalization performance relates to mutual information I(̄X, MLP).
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a probabilistic representation of MultiLayer Perceptrons (MLPs) to improve the information-theoretic interpretability. Above all, we demonstrate that the activations being i.i.d. is not valid for all the hidden layers of MLPs, thus the existing mutual information estimators based on non-parametric inference methods, e.g., empirical distributions and Kernel Density Estimate (KDE), are invalid for measuring the information flow in MLPs. Moreover, we introduce explicit probabilistic explanations for MLPs: (i) we define the probability space (Omega_F, t, P_F) for a fully connected layer f and demonstrate the great effect of an activation function on the probability measure P_F ; (ii) we prove the entire architecture of MLPs as a Gibbs distribution P; and (iii) the back-propagation aims to optimize the sample space Omega_F of all the fully connected layers of MLPs for learning an optimal Gibbs distribution P* to express the statistical connection between the input and the label. Based on the probabilistic explanations for MLPs, we improve the information-theoretic interpretability of MLPs in three aspects: (i) the random variable of f is discrete and the corresponding entropy is finite; (ii) the information bottleneck theory cannot correctly explain the information flow in MLPs if we take into account the back-propagation; and (iii) we propose novel information-theoretic explanations for the generalization of MLPs. Finally, we demonstrate the proposed probabilistic representation and information-theoretic explanations for MLPs in a synthetic dataset and benchmark datasets.

papers.title: Interpretability with full complexity by constraining feature information
papers.research_question: How can we achieve interpretability in machine learning without sacrificing model complexity by constraining the information about input features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for interpretability that constrains the information flow from each input feature without restricting model complexity, using the Distributed Information Bottleneck, providing a continuum of feature importance and fine-grained inspection of feature effects.
papers.conclusion: The Distributed Information Bottleneck provides a novel source of interpretability by illuminating where information resides in the input features, without sacrificing model complexity.
papers.key_findings:
The method can identify the features and feature values most important for prediction by analyzing the optimal information allocation.
It allows full complexity of feature processing and interactions, compatible with arbitrary neural network architectures.
It provides a learned continuum of feature inclusion-to-exclusion and fine-grained compression schemes for each feature.
The method is intuitive to implement with minimal additional overhead, training a single model while sweeping the information bottleneck strength.
It demonstrates utility on a range of tabular datasets, providing interpretability signals comparable to or exceeding other methods.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is a pressing issue for machine learning. Common approaches to interpretable machine learning constrain interactions between features of the input, rendering the effects of those features on a model's output comprehensible but at the expense of model complexity. We approach interpretability from a new angle: constrain the information about the features without restricting the complexity of the model. Borrowing from information theory, we use the Distributed Information Bottleneck to find optimal compressions of each feature that maximally preserve information about the output. The learned information allocation, by feature and by feature value, provides rich opportunities for interpretation, particularly in problems with many features and complex feature interactions. The central object of analysis is not a single trained model, but rather a spectrum of models serving as approximations that leverage variable amounts of information about the inputs. Information is allocated to features by their relevance to the output, thereby solving the problem of feature selection by constructing a learned continuum of feature inclusion-to-exclusion. The optimal compression of each feature -- at every stage of approximation -- allows fine-grained inspection of the distinctions among feature values that are most impactful for prediction. We develop a framework for extracting insight from the spectrum of approximate models and demonstrate its utility on a range of tabular datasets.

papers.title: Examining the causal structures of deep neural networks using\n information theory
papers.research_question: How can the causal structure of deep neural networks be quantified and tracked during training using information theory, and how does this relate to generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a suite of information-theoretic metrics (effective information, sensitivity, degeneracy, causal plane, feedforward integrated information) to quantify and track the causal structure of DNNs during training, revealing how causal structure differentiates with task complexity and relates to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The introduced information-theoretic techniques provide a way to quantify and track the evolution of causal structure in DNNs during training, which may help in understanding their generalization capabilities and moving towards more explainable models.
papers.key_findings:
Effective Information (EI) changes during training, with the largest changes occurring during the steepest reductions in the loss function.
The causal structure of a DNN differentiates according to the task complexity, with networks trained on more complex tasks (MNIST) showing greater movement and differentiation in the causal plane than those trained on simpler tasks (Iris).
Redundant layers that do not contribute to the network's function cluster along the EI nullcline and show little movement in the causal plane during training.
Feedforward integrated information (φ_feedforward) is higher for networks trained on more complex tasks, indicating greater irreducible joint effects in layer-to-layer connectivity.
The sensitivity of a causal relationship between nodes peaks at characteristic weights for different activation functions (e.g., at weight e for sigmoid).
papers.limitation:
Computing EI for large or wide network layers may require many noise samples and is computationally expensive.
The method is applied and validated only on simple feedforward networks and specific activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU).
future_direction: Extending the techniques to different activation functions.
Applying the techniques to unsupervised tasks, recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTMs), and convolutional neural networks.
Using the techniques to assess decompositions and expansions of EI, such as integrated information, and to measure individual instances of causation in DNNs.
papers.abstract:
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are often examined at the level of their response
to input, such as analyzing the mutual information between nodes and data sets.
Yet DNNs can also be examined at the level of causation, exploring "what does
what" within the layers of the network itself. Historically, analyzing the
causal structure of DNNs has received less attention than understanding their
responses to input. Yet definitionally, generalizability must be a function of
a DNN's causal structure since it reflects how the DNN responds to unseen or
even not-yet-defined future inputs. Here, we introduce a suite of metrics based
on information theory to quantify and track changes in the causal structure of
DNNs during training. Specifically, we introduce the effective information (EI)
of a feedforward DNN, which is the mutual information between layer input and
output following a maximum-entropy perturbation. The EI can be used to assess
the degree of causal influence nodes and edges have over their downstream
targets in each layer. We show that the EI can be further decomposed in order
to examine the sensitivity of a layer (measured by how well edges transmit
perturbations) and the degeneracy of a layer (measured by how edge overlap
interferes with transmission), along with estimates of the amount of integrated
information of a layer. Together, these properties define where each layer lies
in the "causal plane" which can be used to visualize how layer connectivity
becomes more sensitive or degenerate over time, and how integration changes
during training, revealing how the layer-by-layer causal structure
differentiates. These results may help in understanding the generalization
capabilities of DNNs and provide foundational tools for making DNNs both more
generalizable and more explainable.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during training similar to biological systems, and how does the early training phase affect the final performance and network connectivity?
papers.core_contribution: Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods during training where early sensory deficits cause permanent performance impairment, and this phenomenon is linked to a loss of 'Information Plasticity' measurable via the Fisher Information of the weights.
papers.conclusion: Critical periods are not restricted to biological systems but emerge naturally in learning systems due to fundamental constraints arising from learning dynamics and information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods: early sensory deficits (e.g., image blur) can cause permanent impairment in final performance.
Sensitivity to deficits peaks during the early rapid learning phase and decreases afterward.
High-level deficits (e.g., vertical flip, label permutation) do not induce critical periods.
The Fisher Information of the weights shows two phases: an initial increase (memorization) followed by a decrease (consolidation), and deficit sensitivity correlates with Fisher Information.
The loss of 'Information Plasticity' (inability to redistribute information across layers) underlies the critical period phenomenon.
future_direction: Exploring whether biological networks prune connections as a consequence of a loss of Information Plasticity, rather than as a cause.
papers.abstract: Similar to humans and animals, deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during which a temporary stimulus deficit can impair the development of a skill. The extent of the impairment depends on the onset and length of the deficit window, as in animal models, and on the size of the neural network. Deficits that do not affect low-level statistics, such as vertical flipping of the images, have no lasting effect on performance and can be overcome with further training. To better understand this phenomenon, we use the Fisher Information of the weights to measure the effective connectivity between layers of a network during training. Counterintuitively, information rises rapidly in the early phases of training, and then decreases, preventing redistribution of information resources in a phenomenon we refer to as a loss of "Information Plasticity". Our analysis suggests that the first few epochs are critical for the creation of strong connections that are optimal relative to the input data distribution. Once such strong connections are created, they do not appear to change during additional training. These findings suggest that the initial learning transient, under-scrutinized compared to asymptotic behavior, plays a key role in determining the outcome of the training process. Our findings, combined with recent theoretical results in the literature, also suggest that forgetting (decrease of information in the weights) is critical to achieving invariance and disentanglement in representation learning. Finally, critical periods are not restricted to biological systems, but can emerge naturally in learning systems, whether biological or artificial, due to fundamental constrains arising from learning dynamics and information processing.

papers.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the origin of the block structure phenomenon in neural network representations? Does it arise from overfitting to spurious data features or does it capture meaningful dataset statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The block structure phenomenon arises from dominant datapoints that share simple image statistics (e.g., background color), which vary across random seeds. The block structure can be eliminated via principal component regularization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The block structure captures real but simple dataset statistics, and its inconsistency across seeds is due to variation in which statistics are captured. Training interventions like principal component regularization can reduce the block structure and improve representational consistency.
papers.key_findings:
The block structure is caused by a small set of dominant datapoints that share similar image statistics (e.g., background color).
The set of dominant datapoints and the specific image statistic they capture vary across random seeds.
Removing dominant datapoints from the analysis eliminates the block structure.
The block structure emerges early in training, but the dominant datapoints and representations continue to change substantially.
Principal component regularization can eliminate the block structure and improve model consistency across seeds without hurting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Focus on image classification tasks and ResNet architectures; it remains to be seen how the block structure manifests in other domains and architectures.
Analysis is primarily empirical; a theoretical understanding is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring how dominant datapoints manifest in other domains and applications.
Applying principal component regularization to distribution shift and self-supervision problems.
papers.abstract: Recent work has uncovered a striking phenomenon in large-capacity neural networks: they contain blocks of contiguous hidden layers with highly similar representations. This block structure has two seemingly contradictory properties: on the one hand, its constituent layers exhibit highly similar dominant first principal components (PCs), but on the other hand, their representations, and their common first PC, are highly dissimilar across different random seeds. Our work seeks to reconcile these discrepant properties by investigating the origin of the block structure in relation to the data and training methods. By analyzing properties of the dominant PCs, we find that the block structure arises from dominant datapoints - a small group of examples that share similar image statistics (e.g. background color). However, the set of dominant datapoints, and the precise shared image statistic, can vary across random seeds. Thus, the block structure reflects meaningful dataset statistics, but is simultaneously unique to each model. Through studying hidden layer activations and creating synthetic datapoints, we demonstrate that these simple image statistics dominate the representational geometry of the layers inside the block structure. We explore how the phenomenon evolves through training, finding that the block structure takes shape early in training, but the underlying representations and the corresponding dominant datapoints continue to change substantially. Finally, we study the interplay between the block structure and different training mechanisms, introducing a targeted intervention to eliminate the block structure, as well as examining the effects of pretraining and Shake-Shake regularization.

papers.title: Explaining Representation by Mutual Information
papers.research_question: How can neural network representations be fully explained using mutual information to decompose them into total, decision-related, and redundant information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based framework that decomposes neural network representations into three exhaustive components: total mutual information, decision-related information, and redundant information, providing a holistic interpretation of representation content.
papers.conclusion: The mutual information framework fully explains the input-representation relationship by capturing all encoded content, decision drivers, and discardable noise, establishing a robust tool for representation analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes total information, decision-related information, and redundant information in image classification tasks using ResNet50, offering more comprehensive explanations than Grad-CAM.
In few-shot learning with a prototype network, the heatmaps for total information and decision-related information show clear differences, highlighting distinct aspects of the representation.
papers.abstract: As interpretability gains attention in machine learning, there is a growing need for reliable models that fully explain representation content. We propose a mutual information (MI)-based method that decomposes neural network representations into three exhaustive components: total mutual information, decision-related information, and redundant information. This theoretically complete framework captures the entire input-representation relationship, surpassing partial explanations like those from Grad-CAM. Using two lightweight modules integrated into architectures such as CNNs and Transformers,we estimate these components and demonstrate their interpretive power through visualizations on ResNet and prototype network applied to image classification and few-shot learning tasks. Our approach is distinguished by three key features: 1. Rooted in mutual information theory, it delivers a thorough and theoretically grounded interpretation, surpassing the scope of existing interpretability methods. 2. Unlike conventional methods that focus on explaining decisions, our approach centers on interpreting representations. 3. It seamlessly integrates into pre-existing network architectures, requiring only fine-tuning of the inserted modules.

papers.title: Absolute abstraction: a renormalisation group approach
papers.research_question: How does abstraction emerge in neural networks, and what is the role of depth and breadth in forming abstract representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that universal, absolutely abstract representations emerge in layered information-processing systems from the combined effects of depth and breadth, and derives such a representation as the unique fixed point of a renormalization group transformation.
papers.conclusion: Absolute abstraction can be defined as the fixed point of a renormalization group transformation, and both depth and breadth are necessary for abstract representations to emerge in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) is identified as the unique fixed point of a renormalization group transformation describing the process of abstraction.
Numerical experiments on Deep Belief Networks and auto-encoders show that internal representations approach the HFM as both the depth of the network and the breadth (variety) of the training data increase.
The level of abstraction of a representation can be quantified by its Kullback-Leibler divergence from the fixed point HFM.
The fixed point representation is data-independent, with data-specific information stored in the parameters that generate data from the internal states.
The HFM satisfies the principle of maximal relevance, a measure of meaningful information content.
papers.limitation:
The numerical experiments are conducted on networks with limited expressive capacity and on relatively simple datasets (e.g., MNIST, Fashion MNIST).
The theoretical framework is minimal and focuses on unsupervised learning from static data, which may not capture all aspects of real neural networks or more complex data.
future_direction: Extending the approach to other types of data and network architectures.
Exploring the implications of the theory for understanding intelligence and the brain.
papers.abstract: Abstraction is the process of extracting the essential features from raw data while ignoring irrelevant details. It is well known that abstraction emerges with depth in neural networks, where deep layers capture abstract characteristics of data by combining lower level features encoded in shallow layers (e.g. edges). Yet we argue that depth alone is not enough to develop truly abstract representations. We advocate that the level of abstraction crucially depends on how broad the training set is. We address the issue within a renormalisation group approach where a representation is expanded to encompass a broader set of data. We take the unique fixed point of this transformation -- the Hierarchical Feature Model -- as a candidate for a representation which is absolutely abstract. This theoretical picture is tested in numerical experiments based on Deep Belief Networks and auto-encoders trained on data of different breadth. These show that representations in neural networks approach the Hierarchical Feature Model as the data get broader and as depth increases, in agreement with theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Anatomy of Catastrophic Forgetting: Hidden Representations and Task Semantics
papers.research_question: How does catastrophic forgetting affect the hidden representations of neural networks, and how is it influenced by task semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that catastrophic forgetting is primarily driven by changes in deeper layers, and that forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that catastrophic forgetting is concentrated in higher layers, mitigation methods stabilize these layers, and forgetting is maximized for tasks of intermediate similarity, providing a foundation for understanding and mitigating forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper layers are the primary source of forgetting in neural networks.
Forgetting mitigation methods like elastic weight consolidation and replay buffers act by stabilizing deeper layer representations.
Forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
Representational similarity (measured by CKA) between tasks is key to understanding forgetting.
A novel CIFAR-100 distribution shift task approximates realistic input distribution shift for studying forgetting.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in developing versatile machine learning systems is catastrophic forgetting: a model trained on tasks in sequence will suffer significant performance drops on earlier tasks. Despite the ubiquity of catastrophic forgetting, there is limited understanding of the underlying process and its causes. In this paper, we address this important knowledge gap, investigating how forgetting affects representations in neural network models. Through representational analysis techniques, we find that deeper layers are disproportionately the source of forgetting. Supporting this, a study of methods to mitigate forgetting illustrates that they act to stabilize deeper layers. These insights enable the development of an analytic argument and empirical picture relating the degree of forgetting to representational similarity between tasks. Consistent with this picture, we observe maximal forgetting occurs for task sequences with intermediate similarity. We perform empirical studies on the standard split CIFAR-10 setup and also introduce a novel CIFAR-100 based task approximating realistic input distribution shift.

papers.title: Information Dropout: Learning Optimal Representations Through Noisy Computation
papers.research_question: How can we learn optimal representations (sufficient, minimal, invariant) in deep neural networks? The paper shows that adding a regularization term related to injecting multiplicative noise can achieve this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Information Dropout, a method that injects adaptive multiplicative noise to learn optimal representations (sufficient, minimal, invariant) and connects it to the Information Bottleneck, dropout, and variational autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: The paper relates the Information Bottleneck principle to dropout, disentanglement, and variational autoencoding, showing that injecting multiplicative noise facilitates learning optimal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Information Dropout improves generalization performance compared to binary dropout, especially on smaller models.
It adapts the noise level to the data and network structure, allowing better use of limited capacity.
It promotes disentangled representations when using a factorized prior.
It yields variational autoencoders as a special case when the task is reconstruction.
It makes representations invariant to nuisance factors.
papers.abstract: The cross-entropy loss commonly used in deep learning is closely related to the defining properties of optimal representations, but does not enforce some of the key properties. We show that this can be solved by adding a regularization term, which is in turn related to injecting multiplicative noise in the activations of a Deep Neural Network, a special case of which is the common practice of dropout. We show that our regularized loss function can be efficiently minimized using Information Dropout, a generalization of dropout rooted in information theoretic principles that automatically adapts to the data and can better exploit architectures of limited capacity. When the task is the reconstruction of the input, we show that our loss function yields a Variational Autoencoder as a special case, thus providing a link between representation learning, information theory and variational inference. Finally, we prove that we can promote the creation of optimal disentangled representations simply by enforcing a factorized prior, a fact that has been observed empirically in recent work. Our experiments validate the theoretical intuitions behind our method, and we find that Information Dropout achieves a comparable or better generalization performance than binary dropout, especially on smaller models, since it can automatically adapt the noise to the structure of the network, as well as to the test sample.

papers.title: A Theoretical Analysis on Feature Learning in Neural Networks: Emergence from Inputs and Advantage over Fixed Features
papers.research_question: How can effective features emerge from inputs in the training dynamics of gradient descent? Is learning features from inputs necessary for the superior performance of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Theoretical analysis proves that feature learning in neural networks emerges from input structure via gradient descent, providing an advantage over fixed-feature models.
papers.conclusion: Feature learning in neural networks depends strongly on the input structure and leads to superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained by gradient descent can learn effective features from input data structure.
Feature learning involves emergence and improvement of features through gradient steps.
Linear models on data-independent fixed features require exponentially large models to achieve similar performance.
Without the input structure, no polynomial-time algorithm in the Statistical Query model can learn effectively.
Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings.
papers.limitation: The problem setup does not include hierarchical representations, which are important in practical data.
future_direction: Extend analysis to hierarchical representations in data.
Further studies on modeling input structure and analyzing feature learning.
papers.abstract: An important characteristic of neural networks is their ability to learn representations of the input data with effective features for prediction, which is believed to be a key factor to their superior empirical performance. To better understand the source and benefit of feature learning in neural networks, we consider learning problems motivated by practical data, where the labels are determined by a set of class relevant patterns and the inputs are generated from these along with some background patterns. We prove that neural networks trained by gradient descent can succeed on these problems. The success relies on the emergence and improvement of effective features, which are learned among exponentially many candidates efficiently by exploiting the data (in particular, the structure of the input distribution). In contrast, no linear models on data-independent features of polynomial sizes can learn to as good errors. Furthermore, if the specific input structure is removed, then no polynomial algorithm in the Statistical Query model can learn even weakly. These results provide theoretical evidence showing that feature learning in neural networks depends strongly on the input structure and leads to the superior performance. Our preliminary experimental results on synthetic and real data also provide positive support.

papers.title: Representation Convergence: Mutual Distillation is Secretly a Form of Regularization
papers.research_question: What hinders reinforcement learning agents from generalizing like humans? How can we enable them to learn robust representations that drive human-like generalization behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies acts as an implicit regularization by improving policy robustness to irrelevant features, which leads to better generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mutual distillation is a form of implicit regularization that improves generalization in reinforcement learning by enhancing policy robustness to irrelevant features and promoting invariant representations.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, improving policy robustness to irrelevant features enhances generalization performance.
Empirically, mutual distillation (DML) improves generalization performance across Procgen environments.
DML leads to more robust representations that are invariant to irrelevant features, as visualized by t-SNE.
The proposed MDPO algorithm consistently outperforms the PPO baseline in generalization.
Ablation studies indicate the improvement is due to regularization against irrelevant features, not merely additional information sharing.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we argue that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies serves as an implicit regularization, preventing them from overfitting to irrelevant features. We highlight two separate contributions: (i) Theoretically, for the first time, we prove that enhancing the policy robustness to irrelevant features leads to improved generalization performance. (ii) Empirically, we demonstrate that mutual distillation between policies contributes to such robustness, enabling the spontaneous emergence of invariant representations over pixel inputs.
